title: The model, stage by stage
text:
The simulator runs one model. Everything in the strategic view, and every scenario in it, is that model with different settings. This guide takes it apart in the order the model is written, so that each piece can be checked on its own.
\[
T_{ij}^{\,y} \;=\; A_i^{\,y}\, O_i^{\,y}\, W_j\, c_{ij}^{-\beta}\,
e^{\gamma_{h(i)} \cdot \mathbb{1}[\,i \in \text{catchment}(j)\,]}\, C_j^{\delta},
\qquad
A_i^{\,y} = \frac{1}{\sum_k W_k\, c_{ik}^{-\beta}\, e^{\gamma_{h(i)} \mathbb{1}[\cdot]}\, C_k^{\delta}}
\]








Symbol
Meaning
Section




\(T_{ij}\)
children from neighbourhood \(i\) modelled as attending school \(j\)
the interior of the matrix


\(O_i\)
children in neighbourhood \(i\) entering Year 7
§2


\(W_j\)
how attractive school \(j\) is, net of where it stands
§3


\(c_{ij}\)
routed walk-and-bus journey time from \(i\) to \(j\)
§4


\(\beta\)
distance decay
§5


\(\gamma_h\)
catchment term, fitted for each catchment \(h\)
§6


\(C_j\), \(\delta\)
competing destinations
§7


\(A_i\)
balancing factor: every neighbourhood places all of its children
§8


\(y\)
entry year, carried as a superscript
§2.7



Two further stages are applied to the \(T_{ij}\) this produces: the admission-number ceiling with the council’s oversubscription priorities (§9), and the re-offering of the children it refuses (§10).






NoteThe year is the only dynamic element, and it enters in one place



Nothing in the equation carries a time subscript except \(O_i\). Journey times, attractiveness, catchment terms and admission numbers are all held at a single point in time, and the year chosen on the simulator’s slider changes only the size of each neighbourhood’s cohort (§2.7). Whether that is the right treatment — and what an explicit time dimension would have to carry — is a question this guide returns to once the static terms are set out.




Show code
ex_zones <- zc %>% arrange(desc(Oi)) %>% slice(1:4)
sch4 <- c("Dorothy Stringer School", "Varndean School",
          "Longhill High School", "Cardinal Newman Catholic School")
data.frame(
  Neighbourhood = c(sub("[|].*$", "", ex_zones$zone), "$W_j$"),
  `Dorothy Stringer` = c(rep("$T_{ij}$", 4), sprintf("%.2f", W5[[sch4[1]]])),
  Varndean = c(rep("$T_{ij}$", 4), sprintf("%.2f", W5[[sch4[2]]])),
  Longhill = c(rep("$T_{ij}$", 4), sprintf("%.2f", W5[[sch4[3]]])),
  `Cardinal Newman` = c(rep("$T_{ij}$", 4), sprintf("%.2f", W5[[sch4[4]]])),
  `$A_i$` = c(rep("?", 4), ""),
  `$O_i$ (2026)` = c(sprintf("%.1f", ex_zones$Oi), ""),
  check.names = FALSE) %>%

The interior of that matrix is what the model produces. The margins are what it is given, or what it fits. \(O_i\) is the one margin that is a count of real people, and it is where this guide starts.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
2.1 What it is
\(O_i\) is the number of children living in zone \(i\) who will enter Year 7 at a state secondary school in the year being modelled. The model is production-constrained on it, which means that whatever else happens,
\[\sum_j T_{ij} = O_i \quad \text{for every } i.\]
Every child is placed somewhere. Nothing is created and nothing is lost, which is why \(O_i\) has to be right before anything else can be.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
2.2 What a zone is
A zone is an LSOA cut by catchment, keyed as LSOA | pre-2024 catchment | current catchment. The city has 195 zones drawn from 165 LSOAs.
The cut exists because the 2024 boundary change runs through LSOAs. Assigning a whole LSOA to whichever catchment contains its centroid would register only a fraction of the children the redraw actually moves. So every postcode in the ONS Postcode Directory is assigned a catchment on each of the two maps by point-in-polygon, and the LSOA is split accordingly. Carrying both maps in the key means the two regimes sit on identical geography and can be compared without rebuilding anything.


Show code
z %>%
  filter(lsoa %in% c("E01016862", "E01016863")) %>%
  transmute(Zone = zone, LSOA = lsoa, `Pre-2024` = catch_pre2024,
            `Current map` = catch_optionZ, Postcodes = n_pcd,
            `$O_i$ (2026)` = sprintf("%.1f", Oi)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "llllrr")

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 2.4 How \(O_i\) is built, step by step
text:
2.4 How \(O_i\) is built, step by step
The code is public/R/01_open_inputs.R in the private bundle, sections 1b and 1c. Its result travels to the simulator as data/open_inputs.rds.
Step 1 — ages become entry years. A child aged \(a\) in the mid-2022 estimates enters Year 7 in \(2022 + (11 - a)\). Ages 0 to 11 therefore give entry years 2022 to 2033, every one of them children ONS has already counted rather than births anyone has projected.
Step 2 — two extrapolated years. Children entering in 2034 and 2035 were not born when the mid-2022 estimate was taken. They are a linear continuation of the five most recent observed cohorts, 2029 to 2033, and are flagged as extrapolated wherever they appear.
Step 3 — resident children become state-sector demand. Not every resident child takes a state Year 7 place: some go to independent schools, some leave the city. A single constant carries that:
\[\text{state share} \;=\; \frac{\text{Year 7 offers made, 2024}}{\text{resident children, 2024 entry}} \;=\; 0.850\]
taken from the council’s published offer total against the ONS cohort of the same year.
Step 4 — a ward is divided between its zones. ONS publishes the age detail at ward level, so each ward’s children are shared out between the zones in it. The weight for a zone is its LSOA’s age-11 population share, divided between the zones that LSOA is cut into by their postcode counts:
\[u_i \;=\; \underbrace{p_{\ell(i)}}_{\text{LSOA age-11 share}} \times
\underbrace{\frac{n_i}{\sum_{k \in \ell(i)} n_k}}_{\text{postcodes in this zone}},
\qquad
O_i^{\,2026} \;=\; \text{ward children}_{w(i)} \times \frac{u_i}{\sum_{k \in w(i)} u_k} \times \text{state share}\]
where \(\ell(i)\) is the zone’s LSOA, \(w(i)\) its ward and \(n_i\) its postcode count. 195 of the 209 zones use the ONS age share; the 14 in the expansion area outside the city fall back to postcode counts alone.






NoteWhy not divide a ward by postcode count



Splitting a ward’s children by how many postcodes each LSOA holds assumes every postcode contains the same number of eleven-year-olds. Family housing, student housing and retirement housing differ enormously on that, and the difference runs along exactly the lines catchment boundaries follow. An earlier version of this work used postcode counts between LSOAs, and the deprivation contrast between the two halves of a paired catchment was almost entirely smoothed away. Postcode counts do the narrower job above — dividing one LSOA between its own fragments, where nothing finer is published.








ImportantCorrected: a split LSOA used to be counted twice



Until this version, each zone of a split LSOA inherited the whole LSOA’s age-11 share as its weight. Ward and city totals were unaffected, because the denominator grew too, but inside a ward a split LSOA took about 1.7 to 1.9 times the share its population implied and the unsplit LSOAs around it took correspondingly less. The splits sit exactly on the catchment boundaries, so the error was concentrated in the neighbourhoods these questions turn on — Whitehawk and Kemptown among them.
The weight is now divided between a split LSOA’s zones by their postcode counts, as in the formula above. The table below is the check that used to fail.




Show code
chk <- z %>% filter(!is.na(prop)) %>%
  group_by(ward) %>% mutate(zone_share = Oi / sum(Oi)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  group_by(ward, lsoa) %>%
  summarise(prop = first(prop), zone_share = sum(zone_share),
            n_zones = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  group_by(ward) %>% mutate(prop_share = prop / sum(prop)) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(ratio = zone_share / prop_share)
chk %>%
  group_by(`Zones the LSOA is split into` = n_zones) %>%
  summarise(LSOAs = n(), `Median ratio` = sprintf("%.2f", median(ratio)),
            Lowest = sprintf("%.2f", min(ratio)),
            Highest = sprintf("%.2f", max(ratio)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "rrrrr")

The city’s zones hold 2,267 children for 2026 entry. That is the model’s entire demand before any child chooses anything, and every intake the simulator reports is drawn from it.

2.6.1 Where the city totals come from
Two different city-wide totals appear in this work, and they have different provenance. It is worth being explicit about which is which.
Offers actually made are the council’s own published figures. Its allocation factsheets are issued after each March allocation round, and the series from 2010 to 2026 was transcribed school by school in the earlier Brighton and Hove allocations analysis. This bundle does not retype them: public/R/01a_factsheet_panel.R re-extracts the year-by-year tables from that document, so every offer, preference and admission number here traces back to a published council factsheet.
Resident children are ONS, as set out in Section 2.3. They are a different quantity from offers: a resident child may go to an independent school, or out of the city.
The model’s city total is the first anchored on the second. The state-sector share of 0.850 is the council’s published 2024 offer total divided by the ONS resident cohort for the same entry year, so the model’s demand is ONS children scaled to the level the council’s own offers imply. It is not a free-floating estimate.


Show code

off <- fp %>% group_by(year) %>% summarise(offers = sum(off_total), .groups = "drop")

  "Resident children, 2024 entry", "ONS ward estimates, mid-2022",

section: 2.7 The slider: how \(O_i\) changes with the entry year
text:
2.7 The slider: how \(O_i\) changes with the entry year
The year slider does exactly one thing to \(O_i\). The city’s projected cohort is turned into an index on 2026, and every zone is scaled by it:
\[O_i^{\,y} \;=\; O_i^{\,2026} \times d^{\,y}, \qquad
d^{\,y} \;=\; \frac{\text{state demand}^{\,y}}{\text{state demand}^{\,2026}}\]

dem %>%
  transmute(`Entry year` = year, `City cohort` = fmt_n(cohort),
            `Index on 2026` = sprintf("%.3f", index),
            Basis = ifelse(extrapolated, "extrapolated",
                           "children already counted")) %>%

2.7.1 Which projection this is, and the one beside it
Two projections of the city’s Year 7 cohort appear in this work. They are built from different data and they are used for different things, so it is worth being plain about which drives the model.
The one the slider uses is the ONS estimate carried forward: the children counted in the mid-2022 small-area estimates, aged forward to their Year 7 entry year (§2.4, steps 1 and 2), and multiplied by the state-sector share. It is used because it is the only one that exists at ward level, and the model needs the geography as well as the total — \(O_i\) is a ward figure divided between zones.
The one beside it is built from children already in the city’s primary schools: Reception offers made seven years earlier, multiplied by the share of a Reception cohort that reappears as a Year 7 offer. That ratio is measured rather than assumed, from the council’s own published factsheets, and it has been strikingly steady — 88.4% across the five most recent cohorts, with a standard deviation of 1.6%. The method is set out in full in how our projection method works, and section 3 of the strategic view uses it as its headline projection because it rests on children already registered in a school rather than on a population estimate.

            Difference = sprintf("%+.0f", reception_based - ons_demand),
            `%` = sprintf("%+.1f%%", 100 * (reception_based / ons_demand - 1))) %>%

2.9 Checked against the council’s own count
Everything above tests \(O_i\) against its own ingredients. The council’s Educational Equity Framework makes an external test possible for the first time: its Appendix 1 counts Key Stage 2 and Key Stage 4 pupils by home ward, assigned from the January 2025 school census. The Key Stage 2 count is Year 6 in that census — the children who entered Year 7 the following September, which is the cohort this term is about. Its lineage shares nothing with ours: census home addresses, against our ONS mid-year estimates.
One feature of the table decides how it must be used. It counts pupils in Brighton & Hove schools. Residents at independent schools, at schools in other authorities, at non-maintained special schools, educated at home or solely registered at a pupil referral unit are all absent from it. So the right comparison is not against \(O_i\), which also holds the children the model sends to Priory, Peacehaven, Seahaven and Seaford Head, but against modelled flows into city schools by home ward. The council’s cohort is a year earlier and about 6% larger than the 2026 one, so what is compared is the shape: each ward’s modelled intake against its counted intake, after that city-wide difference is divided out.

  geom_point(colour = "#1f3b57", size = 2.6) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = ward), size = 3, colour = "grey25",

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
2.10 What to be careful about

The base is mid-2022. Migration into or out of the city since then is not in the counts, and a child who has moved between wards is still counted where they were.
One state-sector share, for every year and every neighbourhood. It is 0.850, from a single round. If independent-school take-up varies across the city — and it plainly does — then \(O_i\) is too high in some places and too low in others.
Ward-level age detail. Within a ward, the LSOA age-11 distribution does the work; how children are distributed inside an LSOA is not observed, so postcode counts stand in for it where a boundary cuts one.
Peacehaven and the expansion area are carried in the open bundle but excluded from the simulator’s zones. Peacehaven Community School is a destination in the model, not a source of demand.
No composition. \(O_i\) is a headcount. Which of those children are disadvantaged is a separate layer applied later, not part of this term.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
2.11 Questions this raises

Should the state-sector share vary by neighbourhood, given that independent-school take-up does?
Should the year slider move the geography of demand as well as its size — that is, should each catchment carry its own projection, as the council’s forecasts do?

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
3.1 What it is
\(W_j\) is the pull of school \(j\) on a family, net of where the school stands. It is dimensionless, scaled so the city average is 1, and it enters the model multiplicatively: doubling \(W_j\) doubles the numerator of every flow into \(j\) before distance, catchment and competition have their say. It also enters the competing-destinations term, because a school’s rivals count for more when they are schools families want.
It is the hardest term in the model to pin down, because everything observable about a school is entangled with where it is. A school with high attainment may be sought after because it teaches well, or because it sits where better-off families already live.

The central one is weighted preferences per place: the council’s published factsheets, pooled over the most recent rounds, counting first, second and third preferences with a geometric discount of 0.5 per rank, divided by the admission number. The paired catchments are why: a family in Stringer / Varndean or Hove Park / Blatchington Mill must rank two local schools against each other, so a first-preference count reads a school families put second as one nobody wanted.
Layer two — the fitted values the simulator uses. The full model does not take any of those five as given. It balances \(W_j\) so that the model reproduces the share of the city’s first preferences each school actually receives, using the council’s catchment-level preference table from its evidence to the Schools Adjudicator. The catchment terms \(\gamma_h\) are fitted in the same loop (§6), because the two trade off against each other.
\[W_j \;\leftarrow\; W_j \left(\frac{\text{target share}_j}{\text{modelled share}_j}\right)^{0.8},
\qquad \text{repeat until } \max_j |\text{modelled} - \text{target}| < 10^{-6}\]
starting from the weighted-preference values, with the result rescaled to a city mean of 1. The exponent 0.8 is damping: it stops the balancing oscillating around the target. This is the same device as the balancing factor \(A_i\), applied to the other margin of the matrix — \(A_i\) makes every neighbourhood place all its children, and this makes every school receive the share of first preferences it is observed to receive.

Figure 4: First preferences for each school, from the published allocation factsheets. Nothing here is modelled. The shaded band is the window the attractiveness term is built from.





Over sixteen years King’s first preferences roughly doubled while Hove Park’s roughly halved, in the same part of the same city. A \(W_j\) built from 2014 would put those two schools the other way round from a \(W_j\) built from 2026. Reputations move, and they can move quickly: a new head, a turn in attendance or results, a building programme, an Ofsted judgement.






ImportantHow the model handles this, and what it cannot do



What it does. It fixes attractiveness at its recent value and gives you a slider to move it. Every scenario in the strategic view that says “a school half as attractive again” is that slider, and §3.6 converts a slider position into points of Attainment 8 so the size of the assumption is legible rather than abstract.
What it does not do. Attractiveness never responds to anything the model itself produces. A school whose roll falls does not become less wanted in the next year of the run; a school whose intake changes does not see its results, and therefore its reputation, move with it. The feedback loop the strategic view describes — a more disadvantaged intake, lower headline scores, fewer preferences, a more disadvantaged intake still — is outside this model. Where that loop is real, a run over ten years understates how far apart schools drift.
That is the clearest case in this document for making time explicit rather than implicit: \(O_i\) already carries a year, and the natural next step would be to let \(W_j\) carry one too.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 3.4 Why there is no exponent on \(W_j\)
text:
3.4 Why there is no exponent on \(W_j\)
The general form of a production-constrained model carries a power on attractiveness as well as on cost:
\[T_{ij} \;=\; A_i\, O_i\, W_j^{\alpha}\, c_{ij}^{-\beta}\]
Here \(\alpha\) is absent, which is the same as fixing it at 1. That is a deliberate choice and it follows from what \(W_j\) is.
A fitted quantity does not need a parameter to scale it. \(W_j\) is not a proxy standing in for attractiveness; it is attractiveness, balanced until the model reproduces each school’s share of the city’s first preferences. An exponent on it would be a second free parameter doing the same job as the balancing, and the two would trade off against each other: any \(\alpha\) can be absorbed by re-balancing \(W\), because \((W^{1/\alpha})^{\alpha} = W\). Fitting both would be fitting the same thing twice, and the pair would not be identified.
It would be needed if \(W_j\) were a proxy. Suppose attractiveness were taken crudely as the number of pupils on roll, or as the admission number, or as Attainment 8 — all of which this work carries as alternative specifications (§3.2). None of those is pull; each is a measurable thing believed to move with it, and there is no reason the relationship should be one-for-one. A school twice the size is not necessarily twice as wanted. An exponent would then be exactly the right device: \(\alpha\) fitted to observed flows would say how strongly demand responds to the proxy, and \(\alpha = 1\) would be a finding rather than an assumption. In the classic retail application that is precisely what the exponent on floorspace does.
So the rule is: balance it, or scale it, but not both. This model balances. A version of it built on roll or on published attainment, which is what anyone without the council’s preference table would have to do, should carry an \(\alpha\) and fit it.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
3.6 What the attractiveness slider does
Each school’s slider multiplies its fitted \(W_j\), from 0.25 to 4 times. Nothing else changes: the same journey times, the same catchment terms, the same admission numbers. Three details are worth knowing.

The multiplier is applied to the fitted value, not to weighted preferences, so a slider at 1 reproduces the model exactly.
The out-of-city schools are not touched by it. Priory, Peacehaven, Seahaven and Seaford Head carry their own fitted attractiveness and a decay on straight-line distance, and the sliders do not reach them.
CoMArt has no preferences, because it does not exist. When it is opened, it borrows the attractiveness of Brighton Aldridge as its starting value, and its slider moves from there.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 3.7 Turning a multiplier into something meaningful
text:
3.7 Turning a multiplier into something meaningful
A slider position is not a quantity anyone outside a model can judge, so the app converts it to the one published number families appear to respond to. Across the ten city schools, the fitted attractiveness is log-linear in Attainment 8:
\[\log W_j = a + b \cdot \text{Attainment 8}_j,
\qquad b = 0.1123,
\quad R^2 = 0.58,
\quad n = 10\]
so a point of Attainment 8 is worth about 12% more attractiveness, and a multiplier \(m\) inverts to \(\log(m) / b\) points. That is how the simulator answers “how good would this school have to be to fill?” — and it is an association, not a lever: Attainment 8 is itself largely a description of who a school admits.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
3.9 What to be careful about

Ten observations. Every statement about why a school is attractive rests on ten schools. The balancing is an accounting identity across those ten; the Attainment 8 fit is a description of them, not evidence about causes.
Attractiveness and location are only partly separated. The balancing asks what pull each school needs given where it stands and how far families will travel, which is a real separation — but it inherits whatever \(\beta\) and \(\gamma_h\) are set to. If distance decay were weaker, the fitted \(W_j\) would be different.
The faith schools have no catchment, so nothing in the model restricts who may choose them. Their fitted attractiveness absorbs the religious criteria that really ration those places, which is why they carry high values.
Peacehaven’s preferences are not published by the council, so both preference measures are filled at the lowest observed rate in the city. That is an assumption, and it flatters Longhill: a weak Peacehaven keeps eastern children in the city.
\(W_j\) does not move with time. A school that improves, or a new building, is a slider position rather than anything the model generates. Whether attractiveness should respond to a school’s roll, its intake or its results is exactly the dynamic question §2.7 flags.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
3.10 Questions this raises

Should \(W_j\) be allowed to vary by family type — by deprivation, say — rather than being one number per school for the whole city?
Should the balancing target first preferences, as now, or all three ranks discounted as the open specification does?
Should a school’s attractiveness respond to its own intake over time, which is the feedback loop the strategic view describes but the model does not contain?

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
4.1 What it is
\(c_{ij}\) is the generalised cost of getting from neighbourhood \(i\) to school \(j\): minutes of walking and bus, door to door, on a weekday morning. It is not a straight-line distance, and it is not a car journey. It enters the model as \(c_{ij}^{-\beta}\), so it is the term that makes a school ten minutes away far more likely to be chosen than one an hour away — and the exponent \(\beta\) that governs how fast that falls away is its own section (§5).
The city has 2,925 zone-school pairs in the simulator’s cost table, spanning 3 to 473 minutes.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
4.2 Where the numbers come from
Every journey is routed with r5r over two networks: the street network from OpenStreetMap, and the bus timetable as a GTFS feed from the Department for Transport’s Bus Open Data Service. The build is public/R/00b_build_travel_matrix.R in the open bundle.

  "Longest walk allowed, either end", sprintf("%d minutes", tm$params$max_walk_time),
  "Longest journey allowed", sprintf("%d minutes", tm$params$max_trip_duration),
  "Departure window", sprintf("%d minute", tm$params$time_window),
  "Percentile of journeys in the window", sprintf("%dth", tm$params$percentiles),
  "Origins", sprintf("%s postcodes", fmt_n(tm$n_origins)),
  "Destinations", sprintf("%d, including the Elm Grove site", nrow(tm$destinations))) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
4.3 From postcodes to zones
The matrix is routed postcode to school. A zone’s cost is the mean over the live postcodes in it:
\[c_{ij} \;=\; \frac{1}{|P_i|}\sum_{p \in P_i} c_{pj}\]
where \(P_i\) is the set of postcodes in zone \(i\). Because a zone is an LSOA cut by catchment (§2.2), the two halves of a split LSOA get their own journey times — which is the point of cutting them.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 4.4 Two corrections the raw routing needs
text:
4.4 Two corrections the raw routing needs
Walking is always available. Where the bus network is awkward the router returns a poor itinerary: about a fifth of pairs came back slower than simply walking the distance, in one case 99 minutes for 4 km. That is a property of the router, not of the city, so every journey is capped at the time it would take to walk:
\[c_{ij} \;=\; \min\!\left(c^{\text{routed}}_{ij},\;
\frac{d_{ij} \times 1.3}{4.35 \text{ km/h}} \times 60\right)\]
The walking pace comes from a systematic review of active school travel: children’s mean walking trip is 1,030 m in 14.2 minutes, or 4.35 km/h, and the circuity factor of 1.3 turns straight-line distance into street distance. The cap binds on 19% of pairs. It is a ceiling on modelled time, not a claim that children walk that far — the same review finds they rarely walk beyond 1.8 km.
A distance model fills the gaps. Where the matrix has no routed value at all, a fitted model of time on straight-line distance stands in. It reaches 0.1% of pairs in the city, so almost everything here is routed rather than predicted.


Show code
wk <- costs %>% mutate(walk_min = km * acc$walk_fallback$circuity / acc$walk_fallback$kmh * 60)
ggplot(wk, aes(km, cij)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = walk_capped), size = 1.1, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(km, walk_min), colour = "#1f3b57", linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey65", `TRUE` = "#d95f02"),
                      labels = c(`FALSE` = "routed time used",
                                 `TRUE` = "capped at walking time"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Straight-line distance (km)", y = "Journey time used (minutes)",
       title = "Where the cap binds",
       subtitle = sprintf("%s of %s pairs are capped",
                          fmt_n(sum(costs$walk_capped)), fmt_n(nrow(costs)))) +
  theme_bh() + theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 5: Every zone-school pair: routed journey time against straight-line distance. The line is the walking time the cap uses. Points above it are journeys the router made slower than walking, and they are pulled down onto the line.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 4.7 The journeys the model does not route
text:
4.7 The journeys the model does not route

The four schools outside the city — Priory, Peacehaven, Seahaven and Seaford Head — are chosen on straight-line kilometres, not routed minutes. The bus network has no direct eastern service to Lewes, so the routed journey from Woodingdean goes through Brighton and takes over an hour, which is not what the families who make that journey do. Their decay is fitted on km against the published 2024 destinations.
CoMArt, when opened, is routed from its old site on the same network and with the same parameters as every other school.
Longhill at Elm Grove has a routed column of its own. An earlier version had no routed times for the site and gave it the average accessibility of a Brighton secondary, which was wrong by about sixty children; the build now stops rather than let that happen silently.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
4.10 What to be careful about

One departure, one day. Every journey is a single weekday morning in the timetable as it stood when the matrix was built. Term-time variation, a missed connection and a cancelled bus are all outside it.
A mean over postcodes. A zone’s cost is the average of the postcodes in it, so a neighbourhood with one badly connected corner shows as slightly worse rather than showing both.
No cars, no lifts, no walking buses. The model prices the journey a child could make on foot and by bus. A family with a car makes a different journey, and that is one reason the east’s figures should be read as a ceiling on difficulty rather than a description of it.
Time is symmetric here. One morning journey stands for the return as well, and no allowance is made for after-school travel.
The cap is generous at distance. A 6 km walk is not a real school journey, but capping at walking time is deliberately crude: it removes router artefacts without inventing a bus that does not run.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
4.11 Questions this raises

Should the zone cost be the mean over its postcodes, or the child-weighted mean, or the best available journey rather than the average one?
Should journeys be routed at more than one departure time, so that a thin early timetable is visible?
Should the out-of-city schools be routed rather than measured on straight-line distance, if a feed covering East Sussex services were used?

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
5.1 What it is
\(\beta\) is the exponent on journey time. It converts the minutes of §4 into a pull:
\[\text{pull of school } j \text{ on neighbourhood } i \;\propto\; c_{ij}^{-\beta}\]
A larger \(\beta\) means families discount distance more sharply. It is a single number for the whole city, fixed at 1.7, and it is the same in every run of the simulator: no slider moves it.
The form matters as much as the value. This is a power decay, not an exponential one: doubling the journey divides the pull by \(2^{1.7} \approx 3.2\), whatever the starting point. That is the standard form in spatial interaction modelling, and it behaves sensibly over the range of journeys a city this size contains.


Show code
bs <- c(1.5, BETA, 2.4, 3.2)
tidyr::expand_grid(beta = bs, mins = seq(10, 70, by = 0.5)) %>%
  mutate(pull = (mins^-beta) / (10^-beta),
         lab = sprintf("β = %.1f", beta),
         model = beta == BETA) %>%
  ggplot(aes(mins, pull, colour = lab, linewidth = model)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = 0.7, `TRUE` = 1.6), guide = "none") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("grey70", "#1f3b57", "grey55", "grey40"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  labs(x = "Journey time (minutes)", y = "Pull, relative to a ten-minute journey",
       title = "A school twice as far away is a fraction as likely to be chosen",
       subtitle = sprintf("At β = %.1f, a 20-minute journey has %.0f%% of the pull of a 10-minute one, and 40 minutes has %.0f%%",
                          BETA, 100 * 2^-BETA, 100 * 4^-BETA)) +
  theme_bh() + theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 9: What the exponent does. Each curve is the pull of a school against journey time, scaled to 1 at ten minutes. The model uses 1.7; the sweep in the open model runs from 1.5 to 3.2.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 5.2 Where the value comes from, and what it is not
text:
5.2 Where the value comes from, and what it is not
It is a judgement, not an estimate. Fitting \(\beta\) properly needs observed flows — how many children actually travel from each neighbourhood to each school — and the council has not released them. A catchment-level preference table identifies the catchment terms (§6, to follow) but not distance decay, because within a catchment every family is at a different distance and the table does not say who is where.
So 1.7 is a central value chosen for a system of this kind: journeys are short, the alternatives sit close together, and it is squarely inside the range this literature reports for school choice. The open model does not rely on it being right. It runs everything across 18 values from 1.5 to 3.2 and reports which conclusions survive the whole range.






NoteWhat would pin it down



A Poisson regression of flows on log journey time with an origin fixed effect returns \(\beta\) with a standard error, from records the admissions process already produces. It is half a day’s work on data the council holds. Every band in the open model that comes from sweeping \(\beta\) would become a number with an interval around it.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 5.5 A second decay, on a different scale
text:
5.5 A second decay, on a different scale
The four schools outside the city do not use \(\beta\) at all. They are chosen on straight-line kilometres with a decay of their own, fitted to the published 2024 destinations:
\[\text{pull of an out-of-city school} \;=\; W^{\text{ext}}_j \; d_{ij}^{-8.0}\]
8.0 is far steeper than 1.7, and the two are not comparable: this one is on kilometres rather than minutes, and it is doing a different job. It is absorbing everything that stops a Brighton family choosing a school in another authority — the admissions arrangements of a different council, the absence of a school bus, the sheer unfamiliarity — and compressing it into the one dimension the fit has. It reproduces the published pattern, which is a low bar for four schools and one year of data, and it should not be read as a behavioural estimate at all.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
5.7 What to be careful about

One exponent for the whole city. Families differ in how far they will travel, and the literature is consistent that the willingness varies with income and with whether a car is available. A single \(\beta\) averages over that, and it is the assumption most likely to matter for the equity questions in the strategic view.
Everything else is fitted given this value. The attractiveness balancing (§3) and the catchment terms (§6) are estimated with \(\beta\) held at 1.7. A different decay would give different fitted values for both, which is why the sweep re-runs the whole model rather than swapping the exponent at the end.
Time, not distance, and not cost. A journey that is quick but requires two buses and a fare is treated as a short journey.
The floor at short journeys. A power decay rises steeply as time approaches zero, so the very shortest journeys carry a lot of weight. The routed minimum in the table is 3 minutes, which keeps it in bounds.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
5.8 Questions this raises

Should \(\beta\) vary between groups of families — by deprivation, or by whether a catchment has one school or two — rather than being one number for the city?
Is the power form right, or would an exponential decay fit the pattern of Brighton’s journeys better? Both are standard; they differ most at the long-journey end, which is where the eastern questions sit.
Should the out-of-city decay be re-fitted once more than one year of destination data is available, or replaced by a proper choice model for schools in another authority?

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
6.1 What it is
\(\gamma_h\) is the bonus a school gets for being in the family’s own catchment. It sits in the exponent, so it multiplies a school’s pull:
\[\text{pull} \;\propto\; W_j\, c_{ij}^{-\beta} \times
\begin{cases} e^{\gamma_{h(i)}} & \text{if } j \text{ is a school of } i\text{'s catchment}\\ 1 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}\]
The subscript matters: \(\gamma\) is indexed by \(h(i)\), the catchment the family lives in, not by the school. Stringer / Varndean families are modelled as following their map more closely than Brighton Aldridge’s families follow theirs, and that is a statement about families rather than about schools.






ImportantThis is about what families name, not about who gets admitted



Admission priority is a separate stage of the model (§9): when a school is oversubscribed the council’s criteria decide who is offered a place, and living in the catchment is one of them. \(\gamma_h\) is doing something different and earlier. It says how much more likely a family is to want a school because it is the one their map points them to — through habit, siblings, the school bus, or simply reading the catchment as a statement about where their child belongs.
The distinction is why the strategic view can find that catchment priority allocates nothing at an undersubscribed school while the catchment still matters a great deal there: nobody is turned away, but the map still shapes what families ask for.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
6.3 How they are fitted
The council’s evidence to the Schools Adjudicator includes a catchment-level preference table: how many first, second and third preferences each catchment’s children gave each school, pooled over 3 rounds. That is a flow matrix — coarse, but a matrix — and it is enough to fit one term per catchment.
The loop is:

Take the current catchment terms and balance \(W_j\) so the model reproduces each school’s share of the city’s first preferences (§3).
For one catchment, try every \(\gamma\) on a grid from 0 to 4 in steps of 0.1, re-balancing \(W_j\) at each step, and keep the value that minimises the Poisson deviance between the modelled and observed shares in that table.
Repeat for each catchment, then sweep again until nothing moves.

The deviance is the right loss here because the cells are counts of preferences: it weights a cell by how many families it contains, so a catchment that gives 400 first preferences counts for more than one that gives 40.


Show code
cal$profile %>%
  mutate(Catchment = unname(gam_lab[catchment])) %>%
  group_by(Catchment) %>%
  mutate(rel = deviance - min(deviance)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot(aes(gamma, rel)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#1f3b57", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = ~ .x %>% group_by(Catchment) %>% slice_min(rel, n = 1),
             colour = "#d95f02", size = 2.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ Catchment, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Catchment term (γ)", y = "Deviance above the best fit",
       title = "Each catchment's own curve, and where it bottoms out",
       subtitle = "Lower is a better fit to the council's preference table") +
  theme_bh(11)








Figure 13: The fit against each candidate value, catchment by catchment. The point is the value chosen: the bottom of each curve. A flat curve would mean the data cannot distinguish one value from another.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 6.5 The two schools with no catchment at all
text:
6.5 The two schools with no catchment at all
Cardinal Newman and King’s are in no catchment, on any of the maps the simulator carries. That is not a simplification: neither school has one. Admission to Cardinal Newman turns on Catholic baptism and practice, and King’s is a Church of England free school with its own criteria and no geographic area attached.
So \(\gamma_h\) never applies to them. Every one of the 866 neighbourhood-to-faith-school pairs in the model has the indicator \(\mathbb{1}[\,i \in \text{catchment}(j)\,]\) set to zero, and their pull is \(W_j\, c_{ij}^{-\beta}\, C_j^{\delta}\) and nothing else. Four consequences follow, and they are worth being explicit about: between them these two schools take 24% of the city’s Year 7 children.
Their attractiveness carries the religion. A family’s faith is not in this model — no published dataset gives it by neighbourhood. What the fitting sees is that a great many families across the whole city name these schools first anyway, and the only term free to explain it is \(W_j\). So Cardinal Newman ends up with the highest attractiveness in the city (3.27 against a mean of 1) and King’s the second (2.57). Read those two numbers as “wanted, city-wide, for reasons the model does not contain” rather than as a judgement of the school.
Distance is the only thing holding them in place. With no catchment bonus, \(c_{ij}^{-\beta}\) is the sole spatial control on where their children come from — which is why they draw from everywhere and why their intakes travel furthest:


Show code
faith_mix %>%
  mutate(School = short_sch(name),
         School = factor(School, c("Cardinal Newman", "King's", "Varndean", "Longhill")),
         Catchment = catch_lab(catchment)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(share, forcats::fct_rev(School), fill = Catchment)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Home catchment") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Two schools drawn from the whole city, two from one corner of it",
       subtitle = "Modelled intake by the family's home catchment, 2026 entry") +
  theme_bh() + theme(legend.position = "right")








Figure 15: Where each school’s intake comes from, by the family’s home catchment. The two faith schools have no catchment of their own, so nothing anchors them to one part of the city.





The children the model sends to King’s travel 41 minutes on average and to Cardinal Newman 33, against 19 to 32 minutes at the eight community and academy schools. That is a real feature of faith admissions, and the model reproduces it without being told to.
They are outside the catchment machinery everywhere else too. The priority-6 rule — a child from a single-school catchment applying outside it — is defined on the catchment design, so it neither sends children to these two nor gives them any standing there. When a boundary is redrawn in a scenario, nothing about Cardinal Newman or King’s changes except through everyone else’s movements. And because they are not community schools, they are rationed by the proportional ceiling rather than by the council’s tiers (§9): the model has no representation of baptism certificates or church attendance, so it treats an oversubscribed faith school as a lottery over everyone who applied.
They still take part in everything that is not the catchment. They compete in \(C_j\) (§7) — Cardinal Newman is the second largest contribution to Dorothy Stringer’s competition term — they sit in every neighbourhood’s choice set and denominator (§8), and families do name them as second preferences, so refused children are re-offered places there: 19% of a catchment’s second preferences go to one of the two on average (§10).






WarningWhat this means for a faith-school scenario



Because the religion is inside \(W_j\) rather than in a term of its own, the simulator cannot distinguish “Cardinal Newman becomes less attractive” from “fewer families in the city are practising Catholics”. Both are the same slider. A scenario that changes either should be read as changing the total pull of the school, and the model will redistribute those children by distance and catchment like anyone else’s — which is almost certainly too smooth a picture of what a change in faith admissions would actually do.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
6.6 What the slider does
The simulator’s catchment slider multiplies every fitted term by the same factor, from 0 to 2. At 0 the map stops mattering to what families name and the model becomes distance and attractiveness alone; at 2 every catchment’s attachment doubles in the exponent, which is a very strong map indeed. At 1 it uses the fitted values.
That single multiplier is deliberately blunt. It answers “what if families follow their catchments more, or less, than they do now?” without pretending to know which catchment would change.

         `At a school in their own catchment` = fmt_pct(100 * rr$in_catch_share, 0))

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
6.9 What to be careful about






WarningThe assumption every redraw result depends on



The terms are fitted on the map families have lived with, and then carried unchanged to any other map. A redraw in the simulator moves which schools count as in catchment; it does not change how strongly a family follows the line.
That is the single most consequential assumption in this work. If families follow a new boundary less closely than the one they know — which the strategic view finds some evidence for in what happened after 2024 — then every redraw result here is too optimistic about how many children the redraw moves. The strategic view reports the halved-term version of the relocation runs for exactly this reason.



The term is fitted on the pre-2024 map, because that is the map the preference table covers.
It bundles several mechanisms. Siblings already at the school, the free bus, habit, and the sense that the catchment school is the school all end up in one number, because the table cannot separate them.
It is a home-catchment term, not a school term. A school in two catchments — none exist today, but CoMArt opening would create one — takes each catchment’s own strength.
Paired catchments are a single object here. A Stringer / Varndean family gets the bonus on both schools, and which of the two they prefer is left to \(W_j\), distance, and the exclusivity populations.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
6.10 Questions this raises

Should the term decay when a boundary changes — a family newly placed in a catchment following it less closely than one that has been in it for years?
Should it vary with how many schools a catchment contains, rather than being one number per catchment?
Would first preferences by small area, before and after the 2024 change, let the normative half of this be separated from the procedural half?

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
7.1 What it is
\(C_j\) measures how much company a school has: how many other schools stand close to it, weighted by how wanted each of them is.
\[C_j \;=\; \sum_{k \neq j} W_k\, d_{jk}^{-\sigma}, \qquad \sigma = 1\]
\(d_{jk}\) is the straight-line distance in kilometres between two schools, and it deliberately carries a different symbol from \(c_{ij}\): nobody travels from one school to another, so routing it would mean nothing. All that is wanted is a measure of how clustered the schools are. With \(\sigma\) at 1 the term reduces to the sum of the rivals’ attractiveness per kilometre they are away.
It enters the model as a power on the pull:
\[\text{pull} \;\propto\; W_j\, c_{ij}^{-\beta}\, e^{\gamma_{h}\mathbb{1}[\cdot]}\, C_j^{\,\delta}, \qquad \delta = +0.3\]
The reasoning is Fotheringham’s: a plain gravity model is misspecified when destinations cluster, because people choose an area first and a destination within it second. Left out, the clustering does not go away — it is absorbed by the distance parameter instead.

text:
7.3 What the fitted exponent does
\(\delta\) was fitted by grid search over -1.5 to +1.5, against the offers the council made in the most recent round, with the capacity ceiling and the catchment term already in place (§6 explains why the ceiling goes in first).


Show code

  mt$delta_fit   %>% mutate(v = "With the ceiling and the catchment term"),
  mt$delta_alone %>% mutate(v = "With the ceiling only"),
  mt$delta_nocap %>% mutate(v = "With neither")) %>%
  group_by(v) %>% mutate(rel = rmse / rmse[abs(value) < 1e-8]) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(v = factor(v, c("With the ceiling and the catchment term",
                         "With the ceiling only", "With neither")))
ggplot(dprof, aes(value, rel, colour = v)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = min(dprof$value), xmax = 0, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "#b2182b", alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(data = dprof %>% group_by(v) %>% slice_min(rel, n = 1) %>% ungroup(),
             size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  annotate("text", x = min(dprof$value) + 0.05, y = 1.55, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
           size = 3.5, colour = "#b2182b", lineheight = 0.95,
           label = "rivals take share\n(competing destinations)") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#1f3b57", "#d95f02", "grey60"), name = NULL) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.8, 1.6)) +
  labs(x = "δ", y = "Error, relative to the same model at δ = 0",
       title = sprintf("Fitted at δ = %+.1f, on the wrong side of zero", DELTA),
       subtitle = "Dots mark each version's best value") +
  theme_bh() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.direction = "vertical",
        legend.justification = "left")








Figure 17: How much the term improves the fit, for three versions of the model. Each curve is that version’s error against the offers made, relative to itself at δ = 0, so below 1 means the term is earning its place. The shaded half is the sign Fotheringham’s argument predicts.





The sign is not the one the term was added to test. A negative \(\delta\) is the competing-destinations prediction: rivals nearby take share. The fit lands at +0.3 — a school does slightly better for having company. That is agglomeration, the pattern of retail parks and restaurant streets, rather than the correction Fotheringham proposed. Negative values are not marginally worse but much worse: at \(\delta = -1\) the error is about 3.1 times its best.
Three things keep the finding modest:

The gain is small. RMSE falls from 22.9 at \(\delta = 0\) to 21.4 at the fitted value, and \(R^2\) from 0.945 to 0.947.
Without the ceiling it does nothing at all. Fitted with no capacity constraint the best value is +0.1 and the error moves only from 68.3 to 68.2 — the grey curve above, which barely dips below its own starting point. What the term appears to explain is mostly rationing.
It and \(\gamma\) are partly substitutes. With the ceiling but no catchment term, \(\delta\) on its own fits at +0.3 and reaches much the same error. Both terms hand extra pull to the same central schools by different routes, so neither is a clean estimate of its own mechanism.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 7.4 Why it is in the model at all
text:
7.4 Why it is in the model at all
Three reasons, none of them “it improved the fit a lot”:

It is the standard correction for a gravity model over clustered destinations. Leaving it out does not remove the clustering; it loads it onto \(\beta\), and the distance parameter then means two things at once.
It moves when a school moves. Rebuilt at Elm Grove, Longhill’s term rises from 38 to 70 — still below average, but no longer alone on the eastern edge. That is a real difference between the two sites and the model should see it. It is also a correction made in this version: before it, competition was measured from Ovingdean even in runs where the school had moved.
It records a negative finding. That a compact city of ten schools shows no competing-destinations effect is worth reporting, and it is at least consistent with the structure: a production-constrained model already normalises each neighbourhood’s choices across every school through \(A_i\) (§8), which is where much of the work the term would otherwise do has already been done.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
7.6 What to be careful about

\(\sigma\) is set, not fitted. The decay on school-to-school distance is fixed at 1. Fitting it as well as \(\delta\) on ten destination margins would be asking too much of the data.
Ten schools. Every statement here rests on ten points, and two tight pairs — Stringer with Varndean, Blatchington Mill with Hove Park — dominate the variation.
It is entangled with \(W_j\) and with \(\gamma\). The sum uses the attractiveness that was itself balanced with this term in place, and §6’s catchment term can do much of the same work.
Straight lines, not journeys. Two schools half a kilometre apart across a railway are as close, on this measure, as two half a kilometre apart on the same street.
Fitted on offers, not preferences. Unlike \(\gamma_h\), which was refitted against the catchment preference table, \(\delta\) was fitted against the offers made — and those are shaped by the ceiling as much as by choice.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
7.7 Questions this raises

Should \(\delta\) be refitted against preferences, as \(\gamma_h\) now is? That is the cleaner question, and this is the last term still fitted against the older target.
Is the positive sign real, or is it standing in for something the model is missing — the faith schools’ city-wide draw, say, which happens to sit in the crowded middle of the city?
Would a nested form — choose an area, then a school within it — represent the paired catchments better than an exponent on clustering does?

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
8.1 What it is
\(A_i\) is not a thing anyone chooses or observes. It is whatever number makes each neighbourhood’s row of the matrix add up to the children who live there:
\[\sum_j T_{ij}^{\,y} = O_i^{\,y} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
A_i^{\,y} \;=\; \frac{1}{\sum_k W_k\, c_{ik}^{-\beta}\,
e^{\gamma_{h(i)}\mathbb{1}[\cdot]}\, C_k^{\delta}}\]
Call the denominator the neighbourhood’s total pull: everything the city offers it, discounted by how hard each school is to reach. \(A_i\) is its reciprocal, and the model then divides the children of \(i\) between schools in proportion to each school’s share of that total:
\[T_{ij} \;=\; O_i \times \frac{\text{pull}_{ij}}{\sum_k \text{pull}_{ik}}\]
This is what “production-constrained” means, and it is the single strongest assumption in the model. Every child is placed somewhere. Demand cannot leak away, and it cannot grow because the city got better: if every school became less attractive tomorrow, \(A_i\) would simply rise to compensate and exactly the same children would be distributed in exactly the same proportions.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 8.2 Computed per population, not per zone
text:
8.2 Computed per population, not per zone
One subtlety: the model does not balance over zones but over origin-populations. In the two paired catchments some families will take one of the pair but not the other, so a zone there carries up to three populations with different choice sets, each balanced on its own.

  count(pop, name = "Origins") %>%
  mutate(Population = ifelse(pop == "either", "Everyone else", pop)) %>%
  select(Population, Origins) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
8.6 What to be careful about

No demand response. Because the row is fixed at \(O_i\), nothing the model does can make families leave the state system, home-school, move house, or appear from elsewhere. A scenario that makes every school worse produces the same 2,267 placements as one that makes every school better. Where a scenario would plausibly change how many families opt out, the model will not show it, and §2’s state-sector share is the only place that quantity lives.
Substitution is proportional. Close a school, and the children who wanted it are redistributed among the others in proportion to those schools’ existing pull for that neighbourhood — the classic independence-of-irrelevant-alternatives behaviour. The exclusivity populations are a patch on exactly this, for the one case where it is known to be wrong.
It absorbs everything the model does not contain. Any systematic pull the equation misses is silently rescaled away by \(A_i\) rather than showing up as a residual. A model that fits well at the school level can still be wrong about why.
It is recomputed in every run. Change a year, a slider, a boundary or a school’s existence and the denominator changes for every affected neighbourhood. \(A_i\) is never carried over between runs.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
8.7 Questions this raises

Should the state-sector share respond to the scenario rather than being fixed in \(O_i\) — a doubly-constrained or elastic form?
Should the choice set be truncated — some neighbourhoods carry fourteen destinations when families realistically consider three or four?
Are the exclusivity populations the right patch for proportional substitution, or should the whole thing be nested?

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
9.1 What happens after the matrix
Sections 2 to 8 produce \(T_{ij}\): how many children in each neighbourhood want each school as their first choice. Nothing in that calculation knows how many places a school has. The city’s demand, laid against the admission numbers and against what families actually named, does not fit:


Show code
pair_either <- d_ai %>%
  filter(pop == "either", catchment == "DS_Varndean", name == "Varndean School") %>%
  summarise(Varndean = sum(wanted))

  filter(year == 2026, name != "Total") %>%
  transmute(name, pref1, pref12 = pref1 + pref2, off1)
dem <- by_sch %>%
  left_join(prefs26, by = "name") %>%
  mutate(short = forcats::fct_reorder(short, pan))
dem_long <- dem %>%
  select(short, `Model: first choice` = wanted,
         `Named first (published)` = pref1,
         `Named first or second (published)` = pref12,
         `Offered, model` = offered) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-short, names_to = "what", values_to = "n") %>%
  mutate(what = factor(what, c("Model: first choice", "Named first (published)",
                               "Named first or second (published)", "Offered, model")))
ggplot(dem_long, aes(n, short)) +
  geom_segment(data = dem, aes(x = 0, xend = pan, y = short, yend = short),
               colour = "grey86", linewidth = 7) +
  geom_segment(data = dem, aes(x = pref1, xend = pref12, y = short, yend = short),
               colour = "#d95f02", alpha = 0.35, linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = what, shape = what), size = 3.2) +
  geom_text(data = dem, aes(x = 0, label = sprintf("%d places ", pan)),
            hjust = 1, size = 2.9, colour = "grey40") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#d95f02", "#9e6a3b", "#d95f02", "#1f3b57"), name = NULL) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(17, 1, 16, 15), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.14, 0.03))) +
  labs(x = "Children or families, 2026", y = NULL,
       title = sprintf("Counting second choices, %d of the ten schools are over-asked",
                       sum(dem$pref12 > dem$pan)),
       subtitle = "Grey bar: the admission number. Named counts: council factsheet, 2026.") +
  theme_bh() +
  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.direction = "horizontal",
        plot.title.position = "plot") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2), shape = guide_legend(nrow = 2))








Figure 19: Each school’s places against how many families ask for it. The model’s demand is a first choice. The published counts show how many families named the school first, and first or second, in the 2026 round. Under the council’s equal-preference system every one of those preferences can win a place.





The model’s demand is a first choice, and a first choice is not the whole story. The council runs an equal-preference system: every school a family names is considered on the same footing, and a family is offered the highest-ranked of its schools where it qualifies. So a school can be named first by fewer families than it holds and still refuse some of them. Dorothy Stringer is the clearest case. In 2026 301 families put it first, against 330 places, and 412 more put it second. Only 264 of those who put it first were offered it: the rest of its places went to families with a higher priority who had ranked it second or third.
The model represents that in two places rather than in the demand itself. Families in the two paired catchments are treated as content with either school unless they are among the few who would take only one (3% would take only Stringer and 6% only Varndean, §8), and a family refused at one school of a pair is offered the other before anywhere else (§10). Counting those families, the model’s demand for Stringer as a first choice or as the partner of a first choice at Varndean is 552, against the 713 families who named it first or second.
The ceiling is where the model stops being about preferences and starts being about administration. It is also where most of the fit comes from: §7 showed that without it the behavioural terms explain almost nothing.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
9.2 Two ceilings
The simulator carries both, and which one is in force is a setting.
The proportional ceiling (rule = "published") cuts every applicant to an oversubscribed school back by the same share. That is the average outcome of a single lottery over everyone who applied, and it is what the published model used before the council’s priorities were added.
The tiered ceiling (rule = "priorities") fills each community school’s places in the council’s own order, and runs a proportional cut only within a tier — which is what a lottery inside a priority averages to. Every number in this guide and in the strategic view uses this one.


Show code
tibble::tribble(
  ~Priority, ~`Who`, ~`Ceiling on the tier`,
  "1–3", "Looked-after children, SEN and exceptional need, siblings",
  "not separable in zone-level flows — see below",
  "4", "Children eligible for free school meals living in the catchment",
  sprintf("with 5, up to %.0f%% of the admission number", 100 * rl$fsm_cap_share),
  "5", "Children eligible for free school meals living elsewhere",
  sprintf("with 4, up to %.0f%% of the admission number", 100 * rl$fsm_cap_share),
  "6", "Children from a single-school catchment applying outside it",
  sprintf("up to %.0f%% of the admission number", 100 * rl$p6_share),
  "7", "Children living in the catchment", "whatever is left",
  "8", "Everyone else", "whatever is left after that") %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lll")

A child who misses a capped tier drops to the one below: an FSM child in the catchment falls to 7, an FSM child from elsewhere to 6 if they qualify and 8 if not, a priority-6 child to 8. Nobody is removed from the queue by missing a tier.






NoteWhat the model cannot see: priorities 1 to 3



Looked-after children, children with SEN or exceptional need, and siblings cannot be told apart in flows between neighbourhoods and schools — nothing in the published data says which children have a sibling already at a school. Most siblings live in the catchment, so they sit inside tier 7, and the comparison below folds the council’s published priority 3 into tier 7 for that reason.
The tie-break inside each priority is a random draw, not distance: the council’s published admission arrangements break ties by random allocation. That is what makes a proportional cut within a tier the right average.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
9.3 Who counts as FSM
The tiers need to know how many children in each neighbourhood are eligible for free school meals. The model has no pupil records, so it uses the neighbourhood’s IDACI score scaled by a single number:
\[\text{FSM share of zone } i \;=\; \min\!\left(1.29 \times \text{IDACI}_i,\; 0.95\right)\]
That multiplier is not chosen. It is solved for, so that the FSM-priority places the model gives at the three rationing schools total the 192 the council actually made in 2026. It puts 20% of the city’s Year 7 children in the FSM group. It is a calibrated quantity, not a measured one, and it inherits whatever IDACI gets wrong about who is eligible where.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
9.4 Against the published outturn
The council publishes, for the three schools that actually rationed in 2026, how many offers went out under each priority. The model was fitted to the total of tiers 4 and 5 only; everything else in this chart is free.


Show code
tier_cmp %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(modelled, observed), names_to = "src", values_to = "n") %>%
  mutate(src = factor(src, c("observed", "modelled"), c("Council", "Model")),
         tier = factor(tier, c("FSM (4, 5)", "Single-school catchment (6)",
                               "In catchment, siblings included (3, 7)",
                               "Everyone else (8)"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, forcats::fct_rev(tier), fill = src)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.65) +
  facet_wrap(~ School, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Council = "#1f3b57", Model = "#d95f02"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Offers", y = NULL,
       title = "The ceiling, tier by tier, against what the council did",
       subtitle = "2026 entry. The council's priorities 0 to 2 are left out; the model cannot separate them from the tiers it has") +
  theme_bh() +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))








Figure 20: Offers by priority at the three schools that rationed in 2026: what the council published, and what the model produces. Only the FSM total across the three schools was calibrated; the rest is the model’s own.





The catchment tier is close at all three schools, and priority 6 is almost exact — it is capped at 5% of the admission number and the model fills the cap, as the council did. The FSM tiers are the weak point: the model gives Varndean the full 30% and the council gave it fewer, because an FSM child with a sibling at the school is admitted under priority 3 and never reaches the FSM tier at all. The three-school total is right by construction; the split between them is the model’s own, and it is too generous where siblings are most common.
54 offers across the three schools went to looked-after children, children with SEN and exceptional need. The model places those children somewhere — it just cannot tell you that this is why.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
9.7 What to be careful about

It is a mean, not a draw. Every number here is the average outcome of the lottery, so no scenario in this work shows the spread. The variance of a real allocation round is not modelled.
Admission numbers are the published ones, not the numbers a school could take. Where a school has taken over its admission number in the past, the model will not.
Only community schools get the tiers. The two academy trusts and the two faith schools keep the proportional cut, so their intakes carry no priority structure at all — and Cardinal Newman has the largest admission number in the city.
The FSM group is a neighbourhood share, not a child. A zone contributes its IDACI-scaled fraction to the FSM tiers of every school it sends children to. That is a reasonable average and a poor description of any individual.
Siblings are inside the catchment tier, which makes the FSM tiers too large at the schools where siblings are most numerous.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
9.8 Questions this raises

Would a sibling term be estimable from the published data — last year’s intake by catchment, scaled by an average family size?
Should the model run the lottery rather than average it, so the uncertainty in a marginal neighbourhood’s outcome is visible?
Should the academies’ and faith schools’ own criteria be modelled from their published admission policies rather than left proportional?

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 10.1 Why a proportional cut is not enough
text:
10.1 Why a proportional cut is not enough
The ceiling in §9 tells each full school how many of its applicants it can take. It does not say what happens to the rest. Left there, the production constraint of §8 would rescale each neighbourhood’s remaining flows to place its children — which spreads a child refused at Varndean across every other school in proportion to how much they wanted each one first.
That is not what happens. A family refused at Varndean who would also take Dorothy Stringer gets Dorothy Stringer. A family refused at Cardinal Newman goes where families in their part of the city put their second preference. So refused demand is re-offered explicitly, in two steps, and only ever to schools that still have room.

A catchment-level table would send every neighbourhood in Longhill’s catchment the same way, so it is modulated by where the neighbourhood actually is. Each neighbourhood’s weight on school \(j\) is
\[b_{ij} \;=\; k_{h(i),j} \times \frac{u_{ij}}{\bar u_{h(i),j}}\]
where \(u_{ij}\) is the share of \(i\)’s children the model sent to \(j\) before rationing and \(\bar u\) is the average of that share across the catchment. A neighbourhood at the Patcham end of Varndean’s catchment therefore sends more of its overflow to Patcham than one at the other end, without anyone having to write that rule down.






NoteWhen a school has moved



The second preferences in the table were given with the schools where they stand today. If a run moves one — Longhill to Elm Grove — the comparison \(u/\bar u\) is made against the flows at today’s sites, so a catchment that the move brings a school nearer to sends it more of its overflow. Without that correction the kernel would be read against a city the families answering it never saw. With no move, the two are the same flow and nothing changes.

The cascade runs 3 rounds, refusing 257, then 25, then nobody. Re-offered demand can overfill a school with a little room left, so the next round cuts it back and re-offers the excess again; the totals fall away quickly because each round has less to place and fewer schools to place it in.
Two things in that chart are worth stating plainly. The largest single movement in the city is Varndean to Dorothy Stringer (86 children by both routes together), which is why Stringer finishes full despite being wanted first by fewer children than it has places for. And the schools receiving the overflow are, in order, Dorothy Stringer, Blatchington Mill, Hove Park — the schools with room, not the schools nearest the refusal.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
10.7 What to be careful about

The kernel is fixed, and it is pre-2024. The second preferences come from the catchment table the council published for the old boundaries. Under a redrawn map the model still uses them, modulated by proximity but not re-estimated.
Second preferences are not a preference for a school with room. The table records what families named when the school they wanted was still possible. A family whose second choice is also full is handled by the next round, which is a reasonable mechanism but not an observed one.
Overflow stays in the city. The kernel has entries for the ten city schools only, so a refused child is never re-offered a school outside Brighton and Hove — although out-of-city schools are in the choice set at the first stage (§8) and take 50 children in 2026 that way.
It is demand, not children. Every quantity here is a fraction of a neighbourhood’s cohort, so “68 children take the partner school” means 68 children’s worth of demand spread over many neighbourhoods.
Refusal has no cost. A family refused twice is no less likely to be placed than one refused once, and nothing in the model records how far down their own list a child ends up.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
10.8 Questions this raises

Should the kernel be re-estimated for a redrawn map, or is the proximity modulation enough?
Should third preferences enter, rather than the cascade re-using second preferences in every round?
Should a refused child be allowed out of the city, as they can be at the first stage?

every journey to Longhill, its competition term, and the reference flows the overflow kernel is read against


Attractiveness, per school
a multiplier on the fitted \(W_j\) (§3.6)
that school’s pull everywhere, and every other school’s competition term


Close or open a school
the set of destinations, including CoMArt (§8)
every neighbourhood’s choice set and balancing factor, and the competition term city-wide


Paired-catchment exclusivity
a multiplier on the share of families who would take only one of a pair (§8)
how many origin-populations there are and what each can be offered


How much the catchment counts
a multiplier on every fitted \(\gamma_h\) together (§6.6)
the pull of a catchment school for the families in it


Places, per school
the admission number used as the ceiling (§9)
who is refused and therefore everything the cascade does


When a school is full
proportional ceiling or the council’s tiers, the priority-6 share, and whether the FSM priority applies (§9)
the ceiling and the cascade, not the demand that goes into them

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
11.2 What a control never changes
This is the important half of the picture. No control in the simulator moves a fitted parameter. The things estimated in §3 and §5 to §7 — the balanced attractiveness, \(\beta\), each catchment’s \(\gamma_h\), \(\delta\) and \(\sigma\) — are fixed when the input bundle is built, and a run reads them. So does the second-preference kernel (§10), the disadvantage pull \(\lambda_j\) (§12), and the two routed cost tables, which are far too slow to build inside a run.
That division is what the sliders mean. The catchment slider does not re-estimate how much families follow their catchment; it multiplies the estimate by a number you choose, and the honest reading of any slider position other than 1 is “what if this were different”, never “this is what it would be”.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
11.3 Where the loops are
Both are in the rationing: one loop, and a fixed sequence inside it.
The outer loop is the one drawn above: cut every over-subscribed school back to its admission number, re-offer the children refused, which may overfill a school that had a little room, so cut again. In 2026 it takes 3 passes (257, then 25 children refused, then none). It stops when nothing is refused or no school has room left; children who cannot be placed anywhere stay unplaced rather than being forced over an admission number.
The sequence inside it is the tier cascade within a single pass: a child who misses a capped tier at a community school drops into the next tier down (§9), in a fixed order rather than by iterating, and the two groups — FSM-eligible and everyone else — are carried through it separately so each places its own children.
A third loop, outside the model, sits in the disadvantage layer (§12): it shares each neighbourhood’s disadvantaged children over the flows it has already produced, spilling any excess where a school would otherwise be sent more disadvantaged children than children.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 11.4 Why it recomputes rather than updates
text:
11.4 Why it recomputes rather than updates
Everything above takes about 0.07 seconds for the model and another 0.06 for all of the outcome measures, on 5,824 zone-school rows. That is fast enough that the simulator does not attempt to update anything incrementally: every change to any control re-runs the whole sequence from step 1. Nothing is cached between runs, so nothing can be stale, and two runs with identical settings are identical to the last decimal place.
It also means the comparisons the simulator shows — this scenario against the baseline, or a school’s fill now against 2030 — are two complete runs compared afterwards, not one run adjusted.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 12.1 The measure that was not good enough
text:
12.1 The measure that was not good enough
The first version of this work measured a school’s intake by the neighbourhoods its children came from: sum the flows, weight by each neighbourhood’s deprivation, done. It is the natural thing to do with a spatial interaction model, and it is wrong.


Show code
dis_fit %>%
  select(short, Neighbourhood = neighbourhood, Published = target) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-short, names_to = "what", values_to = "share") %>%
  mutate(what = factor(what, c("Neighbourhood", "Published")),
         short = forcats::fct_reorder(short, share, max)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(share, short, group = short)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = what), size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Neighbourhood = "#d95f02", Published = "#1f3b57"),
                      name = NULL,
                      labels = c("Measured by the neighbourhoods children come from",
                                 "What the school actually has")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Within a mixed neighbourhood, families do not choose alike",
       subtitle = "Disadvantaged share of the intake, ten city schools") +
  theme_bh() + theme(legend.position = "top", legend.direction = "vertical",
                     legend.justification = "left")








Figure 22: Each school’s disadvantaged intake share: what the neighbourhood measure gives, and what the school actually has. The neighbourhood measure is not a little noisy — it puts the schools in the wrong order.





Longhill is the clearest case: the neighbourhoods its children come from are 19% disadvantaged, and the school is 49%. Its catchment contains Rottingdean and Ovingdean as well as Whitehawk, and the two do not send their children to the same school. A measure that cannot see inside a neighbourhood cannot see that, and a segregation index built on it is measuring residential segregation with a school label attached.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 12.2 So the children are placed explicitly
text:
12.2 So the children are placed explicitly
Two ingredients, and one rule.
Each neighbourhood has a disadvantaged share. As in §9, it is the IDACI score scaled by a single constant, capped at 95%:
\[\text{disadvantaged share of zone } i \;=\;
\min\!\left(1.75 \times \text{IDACI}_i,\; 0.95\right)\]
Each school has a pull. \(\lambda_j\) is how much more, or less, likely a disadvantaged child is to end up at school \(j\) than the rest of the children in the same flow. It is one number per school, and it is fitted.
The rule. Within each origin-population, the neighbourhood’s disadvantaged children are shared over the schools that neighbourhood’s children attend, in proportion to \(T_{ij}\lambda_j\), and never more than \(T_{ij}\) itself — a school cannot be sent more disadvantaged children than it is sent children. Where that cap binds, the excess spills to the other schools in the row and the sharing repeats.






ImportantThe flows themselves are never touched



This layer labels children inside flows the model has already produced; it does not move anybody. Disadvantage plays no part in where the model sends children, in the ceiling, or in the re-offering. That is a deliberate separation — the places are decided by preference, distance and admission rules, and the disadvantage measure then reads off who is in them — but it does mean the model cannot represent a family’s circumstances changing what they ask for.
