Three things in that table need saying.
The Year 7 figures are higher than the whole-school ones at the community schools. That is the free-school-meal admission priority working: it began with the September 2025 round, so a school’s current Year 7 is more disadvantaged than its Years 8 to 11. Fitting to the whole-school figure would have calibrated the model to the policy’s absence. This is the lag correction, and it is the reason the targets are mixed.
The academies and faith schools are fitted to the wrong vintage, for want of a right one. No Year 7 breakdown is published for them. Their targets are the Department for Education’s three-year mean, so if their Year 7 intakes have moved as the community schools’ have, the model will not know.
Longhill’s \(\lambda\) is extreme. 5.9 against about 1 for a school taking its fair share. It has to be: the school is 49% disadvantaged on an intake of only 88 children drawn from neighbourhoods that are, on the model’s own numbers, much less disadvantaged than that. A large \(\lambda\) on a small intake is a fragile thing, and it is the single number the segregation results are most sensitive to.

12.3.1 Why it is extreme: Longhill was fitted across a boundary change
There is a reason this one number is so far from the others, and it is not entirely behavioural. Longhill’s catchment changed between the rounds the model is fitted to and the round it is calibrated on.
Until the 2026 entry year, Whitehawk was in Longhill’s catchment. The council consulted from October 2024, determined the new arrangements in March 2025, and they governed applications made in the autumn of 2025 — so September 2026 was the first intake under the map that moved Whitehawk out. That is the round \(\lambda\) is fitted to.
The model does represent the change. On the pre-2024 map it sends 17 of Whitehawk’s children to Longhill; on today’s map, 0. Geography alone puts Longhill at 30% disadvantaged under the old map and 23% under today’s. What it was actually offered in September 2026 was 49%.
So the pull has to be enormous to close a gap that the boundary change opened. Fitted three ways, the same school gives:

Read that table slowly. Under the old map, with the old target, Longhill’s pull was 1.31 — barely above its fair share. Geography did nearly all the work, because Whitehawk was in the catchment. Take Whitehawk out and fit to the first cohort admitted without it, and the pull has to do the work instead.
The awkward fact is that the first intake under the new map was the most disadvantaged on record. If Whitehawk’s families had simply followed the boundary, Longhill’s share should have fallen. It rose. Longhill is well under its admission number, so a family living outside its catchment who names it is admitted anyway — and on these figures a good many still did. The catchment term suppresses that demand harder than the first year’s offers suggest it should, and \(\lambda\) quietly makes up the difference.
That matters because \(\lambda\) is then carried forward unchanged to 2035. Doing so assumes the transition never completes. Carrying the pre-change pulls forward instead assumes the opposite — that families follow the map at once. The two bracket the answer:

A school that is half disadvantaged or a quarter disadvantaged is not a detail, and the difference in the city’s segregation index, 0.015, is an appreciable fraction of the spread across all the options in the strategic view. Every figure in these documents uses the first assumption, which is the conservative one for any argument that the city is segregated, and the wrong one if Whitehawk’s families are still in the process of moving.
There is a second reading worth holding alongside the first, and it points the other way. Longhill’s intake has collapsed to 88 children. The families still choosing it may be disproportionately deprived whatever the map says, because the others have the means and the inclination to go elsewhere. That is sorting, and it would persist. Nothing here separates the two, and only one thing will: the September 2027 and 2028 factsheets. If Longhill’s free school meal share falls back towards a third, the boundary explanation was right and \(\lambda\) is overstated. If it stays near a half, the sorting explanation was right and \(\lambda\) is measuring something real.

Every scenario in the strategic view is scored on the first and the third of those. A boundary redraw, a closure, a change to admission priorities: what moves is which schools the flows go to, and this layer turns that into a segregation number.






WarningThis measure has changed sign more than once



The direction of a headline finding — whether moving Longhill’s catchment out of Whitehawk raises or lowers segregation — has changed three times during this work, and every change came from a correction to measurement, not to the scenario:

on the neighbourhood measure, it lowered segregation;
on the whole-school fit against today’s map, it raised it;
fitted on the map in force before the change, it was flat;
on Year 7 offers with the corrected neighbourhood weighting, it raises it again.

The scenario never moved. That is a warning about how much weight a single segregation index can carry, and it is why the strategic view reports the direction with the calibration it depends on stated alongside.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
12.6 What to be careful about

Two different disadvantage scalings live in this model, and they are not a mistake. §9’s 1.29 × IDACI is the group with current free-school-meal eligibility, because that is who the admission priority applies to. This section’s 1.75 × IDACI is the broader disadvantaged group — free school meals at any point in six years, plus looked-after children — because that is what the published school-level figures count. They answer different questions and are calibrated to different targets.
\(\lambda\) is a summary of everything not modelled. Sibling patterns, transport cost, appeals, the confidence to name an over-subscribed school first: all of it is inside one number per school.
It is fitted on one year. A single admissions round, on the current map, under the current rules.
A higher index is not a measured harm. The Gorard index describes how unevenly disadvantaged children are spread, which is what the council’s policy aim is framed around. It says nothing about their results. The national evidence in How to Pull the Right Lever is that disadvantaged pupils do slightly better, not worse, in schools with more of them once absence and prior attainment are allowed for, and the strategic view sets out what that means for the options (the strategic view).
A scenario’s segregation number is only as good as \(\lambda\). The model holds the pull fixed while it moves boundaries and schools, which assumes a school’s relationship with disadvantaged families travels with it. For a relocation like Elm Grove that is a strong assumption and it is impossible to test from published data.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
12.7 Questions this raises

Should \(\lambda\) be modelled rather than fitted — as a function of distance, catchment and school characteristics — so it can respond to a scenario instead of being carried through it?
Should the disadvantage layer feed back into the flows, so that a family’s circumstances change what they ask for as well as what they get?
Is the Gorard index the right summary, given how much of the movement above came from re-measurement rather than from the system changing?

The funded roll is the pupil count the school’s 2025–26 schools block allocation was calculated on. The schools block funds Years 7 to 11 only, so a sixth form is not in it.
The pupil-led rate is what one more pupil in Years 7 to 11 brings in. It is the school’s whole allocation less the parts that do not depend on pupil numbers — the lump sum, and where they apply, split site, rates, PFI and exceptional factors — divided by the funded roll. Those fixed parts are why a small school receives more per pupil and loses less per pupil than the average suggests.
Income, reserve and in-year balance come from each school’s own accounts: the Consistent Financial Reporting return for maintained schools (to 31 March) and the Academies Accounts Return for the three academies (to 31 August). The academies’ latest published year is therefore a year behind the others, which the table shows rather than hides.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
13.2 The calculation
For each school, in a run:
\[\text{roll}_j = 5 \times \text{intake}_j\]
\[\Delta\text{funding}_j = (\text{roll}_j - \text{funded roll}_j) \times \text{pupil-led rate}_j\]
\[\text{annual balance}_j = \text{in-year balance}_j + \Delta\text{funding}_j \times (1 - s)\]
\[\text{years of reserve}_j = \frac{\text{reserve}_j}{-\,\text{annual balance}_j}\quad\text{when the balance is negative}\]
Three choices are built into those four lines.
The roll is a steady state. Five year groups at this run’s intake is the roll the school converges on if the configuration holds for five years — not the roll next September. A school whose intake falls today feels a fifth of the loss next year and all of it in year five.
Today’s in-year balance is carried forward. A school that ran a deficit in its latest accounts is assumed to keep running it, before any change in pupils. That is the least-assumption starting point, and it means a single unusual year in a school’s accounts carries straight through.
\(s\) is how much of the lost funding the school can take out of its costs. A school that loses £100k of funding and cuts £75k of spending ends £25k worse off. The simulator uses \(s = 0.75\), the middle of the three assumptions in the strategic view (90%, 75% and 50%). It is symmetric: a school that gains pupils is assumed to spend three quarters of the new money.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
13.3 Worked example: Longhill
Longhill’s funded roll is 719. The model gives it an intake of 88 in 2026, so the steady-state roll is 442 — 277 fewer pupils. At its pupil-led rate of £7,440 that is −£2,061k of funding a year. Taking out three quarters of the cost leaves −£515k, which added to its latest in-year balance of −£168k gives an annual position of −£684k, a deficit of 9% of its income. Its reserve of £531k would last about 0.8 years.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
13.4 Where every school lands


Show code
by_school_path %>%
  filter(year %in% c(min(yrs), max(yrs))) %>%

         short = forcats::fct_reorder(short, gap_pct, min)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(gap_pct, short)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_line(aes(group = short), colour = "grey75", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = year), size = 3.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(c("#1f3b57", "#d95f02"),
                                        c(min(yrs), max(yrs))),
                      name = "Intake year") +
  labs(x = "Annual surplus or deficit, share of income", y = NULL,
       title = sprintf("%d schools in deficit on the 2026 intake, %d on the 2035 one",
                       o26$in_deficit,
                       money_path$in_deficit[money_path$year == max(yrs) & money_path$shed == SHED]),
       subtitle = sprintf("Steady-state roll; %.0f%% of lost funding taken out of costs", 100 * SHED)) +
  theme_bh() + theme(legend.position = "top")








Figure 24: Each school’s annual position at the steady-state roll, as a share of its income, for the 2026 intake and for the 2035 one. The difference between the two points is the falling cohort alone: nothing else in the run changes. Where only one point shows, the school fills in both years and its position does not move.





The ordering is not the ordering of intakes. King’s gains pupils against its funded roll and starts from a surplus; Cardinal Newman fills completely and is still the deepest in deficit, because its latest accounts already show a deficit of £1,740k a year. The model’s intakes decide the change; the accounts decide the starting point, and for several schools the starting point is most of the story.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 13.5 Over time, and under the cost assumption

13.5 Over time, and under the cost assumption

If every pound lost were a pound of cost cut (\(s = 1\)), the cohort decline would cost nothing and the city’s position would simply be the sum of today’s balances, −£474k. title: The model, stage by stage
text:
13.8 What to be careful about

It is a steady state, not a budget. No pay award, no inflation, no energy prices, no capital receipts, no change in the funding formula. All in today’s money.
One year of accounts is the baseline. A school with one bad year carries it forward indefinitely; so does a school with one good one.
Sixth forms are outside it. Four schools have one. Their income includes post-16 funding, so a deficit as a share of income is flattered for them, and nothing in the model moves their sixth-form rolls.
The same cost assumption for everyone. A school with 91% of its income in staff costs cannot shed cost as easily as one at 68%, and the model treats them alike.
Patcham is overdrawn but in surplus. Its reserve is negative and its in-year balance positive, so it counts as having no years of reserve left while recovering. The app says “overdrawn” rather than printing a number that would mean the opposite.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
13.9 Questions this raises

Should the cost assumption vary by school, with staff share as the obvious first candidate?
Should the roll move year by year, as a cohort model, rather than jumping to its steady state?
Should the simulator rebase each school to its actual offers, as the open model does, and show only the change a scenario makes?

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
14.1 What a scenario is
A scenario is a set of control settings and nothing more: a catchment map, a site for Longhill, some admission numbers, perhaps an attractiveness multiplier or a change to the admission rules, and a year. It is applied on top of the baseline, the model is run from step 1 (§11), and the outcomes are read off. No scenario changes a fitted parameter, and no scenario is a separate model.
Scenarios live in two places.

The simulator’s presets — 13 starting points, each a question rather than an answer, which a user then moves the controls away from.
The strategic view’s option set — 29 options in 7 groups, each run in 2026, 2030, 2035, which is 87 runs in all. Every recommendation in the strategic view rests on this table.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
14.4 How to read a scenario
Seven rules, each learned the hard way during this work.
1. Compare in the same year. The cohort falls by about a fifth between 2026 and 2035, and that alone changes every measure. An option in 2035 is read against today’s configuration in 2035 — the do-nothing case — never against today’s numbers in 2026. The grey line in the chart above is always the same-year baseline.
2. A ceiling that does not bind does nothing. Cutting Longhill to 150 or to 120 leaves every measure except empty places exactly where it was in 2030, because the model gives Longhill 70 children and neither number is reached: empty places fall from 583 to 523 and 493, and nothing else moves. An admission number only matters to the schools that fill.
3. Read the measure the option was designed to change, then all the others. Trimming the central schools (Stringer to 300, Varndean to 270, Blatchington Mill to 300, Longhill to 150) was meant to send children to Longhill. In 2030 Longhill’s intake under the option is 70.4 against 69.8 today — it barely moves. What the option does instead is cut 150 empty places and roughly double the children displaced, from 3 to 5. Refused children go to the schools with room that their catchment names second (§10), and Longhill is rarely that school.
4. Small differences in the segregation index are not findings. The Gorard index runs from 0.091 to 0.148 across the whole option set in 2030. §12 showed that re-measuring the same scenario moved it by about 0.01 and changed its sign. A difference smaller than that between two options should be read as “no clear difference”.
5. Know which results rest on held-fixed parameters. Every option keeps the fitted attractiveness, catchment terms and disadvantage pulls (§11). That is safe for an admission-number change and much less safe for a relocation or a reopening, where a school’s relationship with its families plainly changes. Moving Longhill to Elm Grove takes the deprived-journey gap from 3.7 to 0.4 minutes — a result about journeys, which the model measures directly — and the Gorard index from 0.106 to 0.140, a result that depends on Longhill’s fitted pull on disadvantaged children travelling with it to a new site.
6. A slider away from 1 is a question, not a forecast. “Longhill 1.5 times as wanted” does not say anything will make it so; it says what would follow if something did. Package B is Package A with that assumption added, and should be read as “Package A, if it also works”.
7. 2035 is an extrapolation, and the money is a steady state. The cohort projection runs out before 2035 and is extended (§2.7), and every money figure is the position a school converges on if the configuration is held (§13). The 2035 column is the direction of travel, not a plan.

Whitehawk back to Longhill raises Longhill’s intake by 15 children and cuts displacement to 0, and raises the Gorard index by 0.010 — about the size of the re-measurement effect in §12, so the segregation direction is the least secure part of the result.

text:
14.6 The simulator’s presets


Show code
tibble(Preset = names(inp$presets),
       `What it sets` = vapply(inp$presets, function(p) p$note, "")) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "ll")



The starting points offered in the simulator. Each is a set of overrides on Today; the user moves the controls from there.






Preset
What it sets




Today
The city as it stands: today’s admission numbers, today’s catchments, Longhill at Ovingdean, and the council’s 2026/27 admission priorities.


Do nothing until 2035
Everything held as it is, with the cohort ten years smaller. This is the do-nothing case the rest of the document describes.


Longhill to Elm Grove, PAN 150
The relocation, at the reduced admission number, behind the catchments drawn for it.


Hove Park on one site
Hove Park teaches Year 7 at the Valley Campus on Hangleton Way, 1.65 km west of the Nevill Road site its address gives. The council has given notice to close the Valley Campus on 31 August 2028. This runs the first year of the consolidated school; switch Hove Park’s Year 7 site to the Valley Campus to see the same year as it would have been. The total barely moves. Where the children come from does: at Hangleton Way the school draws far more of Hangleton & Knoll and Portslade, and much less of Westdene, Hove Park ward and Poets’ Corner.


Redraw for balance
The power diagram, which spreads disadvantage most evenly of the designs tested, with everything else as it is.


Shrink the system to fit
Total places cut to 1,920, about 5% above the 2035 cohort of 1,835, and shared out in proportion to today’s admission numbers. Move the total or any school from there.


Make the catchment count
Everything as it is, but living in a catchment weighs far more heavily on the choice than families currently behave as though it does. This is the other way to fill a school, and it needs nothing from the school itself.


Make Longhill wanted
Longhill’s attractiveness lifted to Dorothy Stringer’s, everything else unchanged. The question is what it takes, and who loses the children.


Everyone has the same chance
Today’s city with no oversubscription priorities: every applicant to a full school has the same chance, which is the model section 7 of the strategic view publishes. Compare the Catchments and Fairness tabs with Today, which runs the council’s 2026/27 priorities.


The council’s first proposal: 20% open
The open-admissions priority as the council first consulted on it, at 20% of places rather than the 5% it settled on after objections from the six community schools. Watch displacement in the two dual catchments.


The 2027/28 rules: Targeted FSM
The 2027/28 arrangements: the FSM priority narrowed to Targeted FSM, which the council puts at about 56% of currently eligible children. Everything else as in 2026/27.


CoMArt re-opened: three small eastern schools
CoMArt, closed in 2005, open again on its East Brighton site with 150 places, sharing Longhill’s catchment, and Brighton Aldridge and Longhill both cut to 150. Watch segregation, journeys, and whether the central schools still fill.


CoMArt re-opened, and Stringer to 300
The same three small eastern schools, with Dorothy Stringer’s admission number cut from 330 to 300. Does Stringer still fill, and where do the children go?

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
14.8 What to be careful about

The option set is a choice. It covers the levers the council holds and some it does not, but it is not every configuration of them. Something good may lie between two rows.
Every run is a mean. The lottery is averaged (§9), so no option shows how much a real round could differ from its row.
The measures are not weighted. The chart and the tables show every measure side by side on purpose. The strategic view weighs them, and says how; this guide does not.
Options are run on today’s fitted behaviour. A scenario that changes how families see a school — a new building, a new head, a relocation — changes the thing the model holds fixed.

title: The model, stage by stage
text:
14.9 Questions this raises

Should the option set be searched rather than listed — every combination of admission numbers the council could set, scored and filtered?
Should each option carry an uncertainty band from the lottery and from the fitted parameters, so rule 4 can be applied by the reader rather than by judgement?
Should the relocation and reopening options be re-run with the disadvantage pull and attractiveness allowed to vary over a plausible range, since those are the results that lean on them most?

Read one row and the whole model is in it. The neighbourhood’s children (\(O_i\), §2) are divided between schools in proportion to each school’s pull — its attractiveness (\(W_j\), §3) discounted by the journey (\(c_{ij}\), §4; \(\beta\), §5), multiplied up if the neighbourhood is in its catchment (\(\gamma_h\), §6) and nudged by how crowded it is (\(C_j\), \(\delta\), §7) — with \(A_i\) (§8) set so the row places every child. Then the admission numbers bind (§9) and the children who are refused are re-offered somewhere else (§10), which is why the two numbers in a cell differ.
