No design wins outright, and the two that come closest win on different things. Of the 13 measures the current map can be scored on, the flow regions with the council’s pairings kept beat it on 11 and the power diagram on 9. Between them they take 13 of the 17 first places in the table above.

The power diagram is the design to take seriously if the criterion is fairness and balance. It is best on both segregation measures, best on capacity, has no shape faults, and moves the fewest neighbourhoods.
The flow regions win the measures about where children actually go: self-containment, being placed in your own catchment, and the shortest mean journey of any design.
One catchment per school loses on almost everything, and should be read as the negative result it is. The council’s pairings are load bearing.
The two relocation designs lose on travel and on segregation, and win the one measure no boundary can touch — who makes the long journeys.

The measure nobody moves is the one families care about most. First-preference success sits between 70% and 72% across all six designs. Every gain in this section is a gain in fairness of entitlement — who is nearest, who is balanced against whom, who travels furthest. None of it is a gain in getting children into the school their family chose, because that is set by how many places the popular schools have, and a boundary does not create places.






WarningWhat this is and is not



It is a demonstration that the geography could be better, not a proposal. The regions are built from modelled flows and an uncalibrated model. A real redesign would use the council’s own preference and allocation records, which would replace every modelled flow here with an observed one.
Nothing here is in the algorithm that should be. Sibling links keep families together and are a large share of real admissions. Transport cost falls on the council and on households. Existing pupils cannot be moved. Feeder-primary patterns matter to families in ways a flow matrix does not see. Any of these could overturn a boundary drawn here.
The comparison is fair, though. Every design is scored with the same statistics on the same flows and profiled with the same postcode method, so the differences between the columns are like for like even where the levels are uncertain.
And the headline is a qualified one. One design — the power diagram — improves capacity balance, spreads disadvantage substantially more evenly, and moves the fewest neighbourhoods of any alternative. That is a real gain and it is worth having. But it changes how many children get their first choice by nothing at all, and two of the other three alternatives are worse than the current map on deprivation. Redrawing the map is worth doing on its own terms, and only if the redrawing is done on the right criterion. It is not an answer to the problem the rest of this document is about.

title: The Brighton Secondary School System
text:
9.1 Re-opening CoMArt
CoMArt closed in 2005, and the city’s catchment system is partly the shape of that closure (Section 2). The east of Brighton now has two secondary schools, Longhill at Ovingdean and Brighton Aldridge on the Lewes Road, both well short of their admission numbers. A different answer to the east’s problem from moving or shrinking Longhill is to put a school back where CoMArt stood: three small schools in the east rather than two half-empty ones.
The scenario, run on the full model (Section 7.8.3) under the council’s 2026/27 priorities: CoMArt open again on its East Brighton site with 150 places, sharing Longhill’s catchment — the site is inside it on the map in force and on the one before it — with Longhill staying at Ovingdean, and Brighton Aldridge and Longhill both cut to 150. CoMArt’s journeys are routed on the same walk and bus network as every other school, on the same day and settings; re-routing Brighton Aldridge the same way reproduces its existing times to within 0.0 minutes. There are no preferences for a school that does not exist, so CoMArt starts as attractive as Brighton Aldridge, the nearest thing to it.

CoMArt is run as a community school under the council’s priorities, which makes Longhill’s catchment a two-school one and takes priority 6 away from its children. It has no finance or attainment figures, so it is not in Section 6. The same scenario, at any places, attractiveness or map, is in the simulator.

title: The Brighton Secondary School System
text:
10.1 Decisions
Decide about Longhill on a deadline, not on a consultation cycle. The reserve supports about 3.7 more years. A decision deferred past that point is a decision taken by insolvency rather than by the council.
Treat the instruments as a package. Section 8 shows they compose. Section 3 shows the cohort keeps falling regardless. Adjusting a single admission number and waiting to see what happens will consume years the finances do not have.
Stop pointing families at Attainment 8. The council publishes the admissions guide, and it tells parents to look at each school’s “National Curriculum test results, public exam results” (2027 to 2028). Section 5 shows families track the headline score at 84% and the value-added measure at 20%. Publishing a contextualised measure alongside the headline would cost nothing and would begin to unwind a self-fulfilling loop the authority currently sustains.
Treat transport as an admissions instrument. Section 4 found 29 neighbourhoods that can reach no school place inside 30 minutes, concentrated in the more deprived third of the city. A bus timetable can widen real choice without taking anything from anyone — which is more than can be said for any boundary change.

title: The Brighton Secondary School System
text:
10.2 Questions raised in this document
Numbered questions appear in the sections above where the evidence raises them. They are gathered here so they can be put as a set. None requires new research; each is answerable from records the council already holds.

Why is the catchment forecast wrong in Longhill and in Hove Park / Blatchington Mill, in opposite directions? (§3.4) In 2026 Longhill was forecast 162 and received 81, while Hove Park / Blatchington Mill was 42 places under. The second has a candidate explanation in the neighbouring PACA over-forecast; the first does not.
Which neighbourhoods did the priority-6 places go to, and what did they do to the social mix of the community schools’ intakes?

In the full model it makes almost no difference to how mixed intakes are, and who uses it varies by catchment. The council holds the offers and the home postcodes to test both.

title: The Brighton Secondary School System
section: 10.3 Data the council could simply publish
text:
10.3 Data the council could simply publish
Every “this cannot be done on published data” note in this document resolves to a small number of releases. None requires new collection; all are aggregates of data the council already holds.








#
What
What it would settle




1
Home LSOA of every applicant, by year and allocated school
Calibrate \(\beta\); replace every band in section 8 with an estimate


2
Full preference ordering, anonymised, by year
Turn section 5’s ten-point association into a discrete-choice model


3
Allocated school by home LSOA, including schools outside the city
Measure the actual outflow the council’s forecasts assume


4
Criterion under which each place was allocated
Establish directly which criteria bind, rather than inferring it


5
Children allocated a school they did not name, by school, year and home catchment
Test the council’s stated “nearest school with places” practice, and complete each school’s intake: the published offer counts are counted by preference rank, so a child placed at a school they did not name does not appear in them


6
Journey actually made, or at least distance, per allocation
Separate potential accessibility from realised accessibility


7
Offers by admission criterion for every school, every year
The admissions guide gives the priority breakdown only for the schools that rationed places; the rest would show how the tiered ceiling behaves where it barely binds


8
Offers to children living outside the city, by school
The model contains Brighton & Hove children only. Schools that admit across a wider area — the faith schools above all — fill some places the model cannot see


9
The catchment preference table for each round separately, not pooled
Let each school’s attractiveness be fitted year by year, so a change such as a new Ofsted judgement shows up when it happens rather than being averaged away


10
In each paired catchment, how many applicants named one school of the pair, both, or neither
Fit the share who would take only one of the pair each year, rather than holding it fixed



The last four follow from where the model’s remaining error sits. Its intakes for September 2026 match the council’s offers closely at most schools and miss at two: it gives Brighton Aldridge too few children and Hove Park too many (model guide). The published factsheets show why both are hard for a model fitted to a pooled table. Brighton Aldridge’s first preferences rose from 83 to 128 in the first round after its April 2025 Ofsted judgement, and Hove Park’s second preferences fell from 242 to 171 in the same round. A model whose attractiveness is an average of earlier rounds cannot follow a change that happens in one. Releases 9 and 10 would let it, and releases 5, 7 and 8 would let the model be checked against every child placed rather than only those offered a school they named.
LSOAs average about 1,500 residents and 650 households. A cohort-year count at LSOA level is not disclosive in the way a postcode-level count would be, and the council already publishes LSOA-level material elsewhere.

10.3.1 What one small table already settled
The case for these releases is not hypothetical, because one of them has in effect already happened. Appendix 1 of the council’s Educational Equity Framework, prepared for the People Overview & Scrutiny Committee, counts Key Stage 2 and Key Stage 4 pupils by home ward and by middle super output area, taken from the January 2025 school census. It was published to describe attainment, not pupil numbers, and the counts sit in it as a by-product.
Those counts are the first external check this model’s origins have ever had. Every other test in this document tests where the model sends children; nothing tested how many it starts with in each neighbourhood, and that is built from ONS ward estimates and a single state-sector share for the whole city. Set the council’s Key Stage 2 count against modelled intakes into city schools, ward by ward, and the geography holds: the two correlate at 0.96. The flat share does not. It implies a share of each ward’s children in city schools running from about 0.66 in Round Hill to about 1.21 in Woodingdean, against the 0.85 the model applies everywhere. Rebuilding the model’s origins on per-ward shares moves its intakes closer to the offers the city’s schools actually made in September 2026, on every measure of fit, although the offers play no part in deriving the shares. The model guide sets out the comparison in full; the results in this document still use the flat share.
Two things follow. The first is a correction the council could make to its own place planning: how many of an area’s children take a city state school place varies far more across the city than a single rate allows, and the variation is large enough to change which schools look full. The second is the general point. A table published for another purpose entirely, containing nothing more sensitive than counts of pupils by ward, answered a question that had been stated as unanswerable. The ten releases above are of the same kind.

title: The Brighton Secondary School System
text:
10.4 Why now
The cohort projections in section 3 are not forecasts. Those children are in the city’s primary schools today. The financial position in section 6 has a horizon of about 3.7 years. The decisions in front of the council will shape the school system for the next fifteen to twenty years, and they are being taken without a picture of the whole system.
This document is an attempt to supply as much of that picture as published data allows. It stops well short of what the council’s own records would support — and the offer to do that work, properly and in the open, stands.

title: The Brighton Secondary School System
text:
11.2 Priority 1: keeping Longhill open
No option tested makes Longhill pay its way. On section 6’s funding assumptions Longhill breaks even at about 162 children a year; each child is worth about £9,300 a year to its balance. Today it takes 88 in 2026 and 63 by 2035. The best of the options below take it to around a hundred for a few years and to the eighties by 2035. Keeping Longhill open is therefore a decision to run a smaller school at a cost — to plan its staffing and curriculum for about a hundred children a year rather than to wait for 150 — and the council should take it as that, openly, rather than as a bet on recovery.
Cutting its admission number removes empty places; it does not add children. At 150 or 120 places Longhill takes exactly the children it takes at 210, and its balance is unchanged. The cut is still worth making — 60 empty places a year gone from the community schools — but it is housekeeping, not rescue.
The levers that do move children, ranked by what they add in 2030:

Whitehawk back in Longhill’s catchment adds 15 children (103 in 2026, 76 in 2035, against 88 and 63), and keeps most of that gain as the cohort falls. It barely changes journeys, and Priority 3 shows it lowers displacement. It raises segregation, by more than any other option short of moving a school (Priority 2).
Moving to Elm Grove with redrawn catchments adds 16 in 2030 and 18 in 2026, more than any other single change the council controls, and the map drawn round the new site puts 4 of the 6 Whitehawk neighbourhoods back in Longhill’s catchment. It needs a new site, which is not costed here, and it raises segregation (Priority 2).
Making Longhill half as attractive again adds 18. On section 5.4’s fit that is about 3.6 points of Attainment 8, which a school with a falling roll is poorly placed to deliver.
Cardinal Newman and King’s taking fewer children — Cardinal Newman at 270 and King’s at 150 — adds 5 in 2030 and 17 in 2026, and does more for the community schools’ finances than any other single change the council does not control: their combined balance improves by £0.8m a year by 2035. Cardinal Newman at 300 alone does about half of that.
Trimming the full central schools — Stringer to 300, Varndean to 270, Blatchington Mill to 300 — adds 13 in 2026 and nothing by 2030, because by then the falling cohort has left those schools with room of their own. It is a lever for the next two or three rounds only, and it lengthens journeys for the children it moves unless it goes with a redraw that gives them a nearer school.

Asking Brighton Aldridge and Portslade Aldridge to shrink does nothing for Longhill. Neither fills, so a lower number only removes their own empty places.

title: The Brighton Secondary School System
text:
11.3 Priority 2: access and segregation
These are two different things, and the options that help one often hurt the other.
Access — how much further deprived children travel than everyone else — is improved most by putting a school where they live. With Longhill at Elm Grove the gap falls from 3.7 to 0.4 minutes; with CoMArt open, to 2.7. Nothing else in the table moves it by more than half a minute.
For Whitehawk the move does what the redraw cannot. With Longhill at Elm Grove, Whitehawk’s children travel 30 minutes on average in 2026 against 54 today, and its disadvantaged children 22 against 54. Returning Whitehawk to Longhill’s catchment with the school at Ovingdean leaves its disadvantaged children at 52 minutes, because Ovingdean is no nearer to them than Varndean is.
Segregation is lowest where the intakes are mixed, and a school placed among deprived neighbourhoods recruits from them: Gorard’s index rises from 0.106 to 0.140 with Longhill at Elm Grove and to 0.107 with CoMArt open (Section 9.1).
Returning Whitehawk to Longhill’s catchment raises segregation. In 2030 the index is 0.106 today and 0.116 with the redraw; in 2026, 0.116 and 0.130. That is the largest rise of any option the council can take without moving or opening a school. Earlier versions of this section found first that the redraw lowered segregation and then that it barely moved it; the box below sets out what changed, and how far the finding now holds.






NoteDoes returning Whitehawk to Longhill change segregation?



Who lives there. The 2024 catchment change moved 6 small areas around CoMArt’s old site in Whitehawk out of Longhill’s catchment and into Stringer / Varndean’s. About 78 children a year live in them, and 75% of them are disadvantaged — against 26% across the city, 23% in the rest of Stringer / Varndean’s catchment, and 26% in Longhill’s.
Where their children go. Today 37 go to Varndean and 25 to Stringer. Returned to Longhill’s catchment, 17 go to Longhill — in the model almost all of them disadvantaged ones, for the reason set out below — and Cardinal Newman takes 18 rather than 6. For the children who go to Longhill the journey is about 34 minutes, against 49 to Varndean.

What it does to the intakes. Across the city 26.5% of pupils are disadvantaged. Longhill’s intake, already above that at 49.4%, rises to 57.7%, which adds to the index. Varndean’s, also above it today at 30.0%, falls to 24.8%, passing below it. Stringer’s goes from 25.5% to 22.4%, further below it again. All three schools end further from the city’s share than they started, and Gorard’s index measures exactly that: it is 0.116 today and 0.130 with the redraw in 2026, 0.106 and 0.116 in 2030.
Why earlier versions said otherwise.

  filter(year == 2026) %>%
  select(measure, map, gorard, longhill_share, varndean_share) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = map, values_from = c(gorard, longhill_share, varndean_share)) %>%
  transmute(`Disadvantaged pupils counted` = measure,
            `Index, today` = sprintf("%.3f", gorard_today),
            `With Whitehawk back` = sprintf("%.3f", gorard_whitehawk),
            `Longhill` = sprintf("%s → %s", fmt_pct(100 * longhill_share_today, 0), fmt_pct(100 * longhill_share_whitehawk, 0)),
            `Varndean` = sprintf("%s → %s", fmt_pct(100 * varndean_share_today, 0), fmt_pct(100 * varndean_share_whitehawk, 0))) %>%

Scored by the neighbourhoods their children come from, Varndean looked the more deprived school and Longhill the less, so moving Whitehawk looked like evening them out. The published figures put them the other way round, and the second version fitted each school’s pull on disadvantaged children to those figures — but on today’s map. The published figures are whole-school averages for cohorts admitted before the 2024 map and the new priorities, when Whitehawk was in Longhill’s catchment. Fitted on today’s map, Longhill’s pull (2.26) stood in for Whitehawk children it no longer admits, and Varndean’s (0.49) held down the ones it now does; moving Whitehawk then looked like concentrating disadvantage at Longhill. Fitted on the map and rules those cohorts were admitted under, the pulls are 1.31 and 0.90, and the redraw barely moves the index — but that fit still misses what the new rules do. Fitted to the first Year 7 offers under today’s map and priorities, the model’s measure, Longhill’s pull is far stronger, 5.95, because 49% of its September 2026 offers went to children eligible for free school meals; Varndean’s is 0.68. On that measure the redraw raises the index a little, because the model sends Longhill almost only the disadvantaged Whitehawk children: 17 of 17.
How firm that is. As fitted, the redraw changes the index by +0.013; at half the fitted pull by +0.004; with no pull by -0.011. It rises at the fitted pull and still rises at half of it, and only reverses when the pull is removed altogether — which is the version that no longer reproduces the council’s offers. The direction is as firm as the fitted pull is, and the size of it is not. Longhill’s pull rests on a single year of offers at a school that made fewer than a hundred of them on offer day, and it implies that almost every Whitehawk family choosing Longhill would be disadvantaged. A second year of Year 7 offers would test it; the published whole-school figures will not show the 2024 map in full until every year group has been admitted under it, in 2029-30.
What that leaves. The redraw is a genuine trade. Against the rise in the index sit a shorter journey for the children who would take a Longhill place, 15 more children a year for Longhill by 2030, and less displacement. For comparison, the whole pre-2024 map scores 0.119 in 2026, against 0.116 today. And a more or less mixed intake is not the same as better or worse results for the children in it: most of the difference between schools’ headline scores reflects who they teach rather than what they add (Section 2.4).


Priority 6 makes almost no difference. Switched off, the index is 0.106; at 20% it is 0.106 (the priority-6 subsection of section 8). Removing all oversubscription priorities gives 0.098 and displaces 33 children in 2026 against 7.
The power diagram raises segregation on this model — 0.096 — and costs Longhill 1 children. It is not recommended on this evidence.

title: The Brighton Secondary School System
text:
11.4 Priority 3: catchments, journeys and displacement
For parents the first thing is a short journey to a school near home and friends, and the second is not being displaced from it.
Displacement is small and falling. 7 children in 2026 and 3 in 2030 would have taken a place in their catchment and cannot. Options that trim the full schools hard raise it — to 76 in 2026 with Stringer at 270, Varndean at 240 and Blatchington Mill at 270 — and so does removing the priorities. Whitehawk back to Longhill lowers it, to 4 in 2026, because the Whitehawk families who would be refused at a full central school now have a catchment school with room.
The share of children at a school in their own catchment is raised most by the faith schools taking fewer — 62% with Cardinal Newman at 270 and King’s at 150, against 58% — because every child they do not take goes to a catchment school instead, and usually a nearer one: the longest journeys fall to 53 minutes from 54.
Closing Longhill is the option parents would pay most for. It saves the most money — the community schools’ balance is −£0.5m in 2026 against −£1.4m, partly because Longhill’s own deficit leaves the books — but the longest journeys lengthen to 59 minutes, the share travelling over 40 minutes rises to 29%, and more children leave the city: 75 in 2030 against 61. It also lowers segregation more than any other option in the table, to 0.091 against 0.106: Longhill’s Year 7 intake is among the most disadvantaged in the city, and its children would spread across schools with less disadvantaged ones. That is a statistic about intakes, not a benefit to the children who would travel further. It is the counterfactual against which keeping Longhill open is a choice to spend money on shorter journeys in the east.

By 2035 the city carries 720 empty Year 7 places a year, 493 of them in the community schools. Removing them from the community schools alone makes the community schools worse off: their balance goes from −£4.4m to −£5.6m, because the children they no longer have room for go to the academies and faith schools, and 77 are displaced from their catchment. Removing places from every school in proportion does the opposite: −£4.0m, with 6 displaced and 63% of children at a catchment school. A viable system in 2035 is one in which the schools the council does not run shrink with the ones it does, and the council’s case for asking them rests on exactly this comparison.

title: The Brighton Secondary School System
text:
11.6 All three together
Where the priorities agree.

Cardinal Newman and King’s taking fewer helps Priority 1 and Priority 3 together, and the community schools’ finances most of all. It needs the dioceses’ agreement, and the case to put to them is that a city whose cohort is falling cannot keep every school full, and that the schools it does not run are part of the same system.
Reviewing priority 6 touches little. It makes almost no difference to segregation and a small one to displacement, and it gives something real — a route into the popular schools for the children of single-school catchments who use it. The case for keeping it at 5% is as good as the case against.

Where they compete, and which should give.

Longhill and journeys against mixed intakes. Returning Whitehawk to Longhill’s catchment gives Longhill 15 more children a year by 2030, lowers displacement and shortens the journeys of the children it moves — and raises the segregation index from 0.106 to 0.116, because the neighbourhoods it moves are 75% disadvantaged against 26% across the city. Which way that trade should go is a judgement, and the council should make it knowing both halves — and knowing that the higher index counts against the redraw under the council’s aim of evening out intakes, not on the evidence about disadvantaged pupils’ results (Section 2.3.1).
Access against segregation. Elm Grove all but closes the gap between deprived children’s journeys and everyone else’s, and it concentrates disadvantaged children in one school: the index rises from 0.106 to 0.140. A review of how to even out disadvantaged children’s chances has to choose between those two measures, because relocation improves one and worsens the other. This document’s evidence leans towards access: most of what separates schools’ headline results arrives with the children rather than being added by the school (Section 2.4), so a more mixed intake is a weak lever on outcomes, while the journey is made by every child twice a day. For disadvantaged pupils the national evidence goes further: they do slightly better, not worse, where they are concentrated in a school organised for them, and Brighton Aldridge is the city’s own example (Section 2.3.1). What the document cannot show is whether shorter journeys raise attendance; the council’s records could.
Longhill against short journeys. Trimming the central schools helps Longhill for two or three years and lengthens journeys for the children moved. It should be done only with the Whitehawk redraw, and only while those schools are full.
Money against journeys. Closing Longhill is the cheapest system and the one with the longest journeys in the east. Keeping it open is worth doing only as a deliberate choice to pay for shorter journeys and a school in the east, sized and staffed for the children it will get.


11.6.1 The recommendation
If the council’s inequalities review puts evening out disadvantaged children’s chances first, the order of the recommendations changes. The earlier version of this section treated a move to Elm Grove as an access decision to be weighed against its cost to Longhill. On the full model with the catchments redrawn, it is the option that does most for access and most for Longhill’s roll, and the map drawn round it settles the Whitehawk question as part of a redesign. So it leads.

Make a smaller Longhill at the top of Elm Grove the lead option, and test it properly. At 150 places with the catchments redrawn round it, Longhill takes 106 children in 2026 and 86 in 2030, against 88 and 70 today; deprived children stop travelling further than everyone else, a gap of 0.4 minutes against 3.7; Whitehawk’s disadvantaged children’s journeys fall from 54 to 22 minutes; and the new map puts 4 of the 6 Whitehawk neighbourhoods back in Longhill’s catchment. A move needs a new map in any case, so Whitehawk’s return comes as part of a redesign built round a new school rather than as a stand-alone reversal of the 2024 change. The costs belong in the same paper: a site, not costed here; a segregation index of 0.140 against 0.106; 337 children a year in neighbourhoods that change catchment; longer journeys for Rottingdean, Saltdean and Woodingdean, more of whose children leave the city (66 from across the city in 2030 against 61); and a school that still does not break even.
If the site cannot be had, return Whitehawk to Longhill’s catchment on its own. It gives Longhill 15 children a year by 2030 and lowers displacement, and it raises the segregation index from 0.106 to 0.116. It also does little for Whitehawk’s journeys while the school is at Ovingdean: its disadvantaged children travel 52 minutes against 54 now. It is the fallback, not the first choice.
Set Longhill’s admission number at 150, on either site, and plan its budget and staffing for the children it will get — about a hundred at Ovingdean, somewhat more at Elm Grove — not for 150. Put the gap between that and break-even — about £0.9m a year at Ovingdean in 2030 and £0.7m at Elm Grove — to members as the cost of keeping a school in the east, and decide it as that.
Ask Cardinal Newman to reduce to 300, and King’s to 150, and Brighton Aldridge to 150, and make the case for each school in the city giving up places in proportion by 2030. With Longhill at Elm Grove these asks add most to its roll.
Trim Stringer, Varndean and Blatchington Mill only if Longhill stays at Ovingdean and only with a catchment redraw — to 300, 270 and 300, for the next two or three rounds while they are full, with Whitehawk returned to Longhill’s catchment. With Longhill at Elm Grove the trims add few children in the model’s runs and raise displacement.
Publish where priority 6’s places went, so what it does to segregation can be measured rather than modelled.
Ask the inequalities review to settle the measure. Relocation shortens disadvantaged children’s journeys and concentrates them in one school. Whether evening out chances means the first or the second, and whether shorter journeys raise attendance, are questions the review can answer from the council’s own records and this document cannot. It should weigh the national evidence that disadvantaged pupils do no worse — slightly better — in schools where they are concentrated and well served (Section 2.3.1), before treating a more concentrated intake as a cost.

Together — Longhill at Elm Grove at 150 with the catchments redrawn, Cardinal Newman at 300, King’s at 150 and Brighton Aldridge at 150 — that package gives Longhill 117 children in 2026 and 91 in 2030, against 88 and 70; a segregation index of 0.138 against 0.106; 6 children displaced in 2026 against 7; 61% at a catchment school against 58%; and, in 2026, longest journeys of 53 minutes against 53; and a deprived-journey gap of 0.5 minutes against 3.7. It does not make Longhill break even; that needs a decision about money. Without the move, the best package tested — Whitehawk back to Longhill, Longhill at 150, the central trims, no priority 6, Cardinal Newman at 300 and Brighton Aldridge at 150 — gives Longhill 129 in 2026 and 90 in 2030, and leaves the deprived-journey gap at 3.5 minutes: only a school nearer to them, or better buses, closes that (Section 10.1).






WarningWhat this rests on



Every number here is from a model calibrated to published catchment totals, not to individual applications. The finances are a steady state five years out, with a school shedding three quarters of the cost of a pupil it loses. The catchment terms are carried to redrawn maps at the strength families follow the maps they have, which is what decides every redraw result above. Segregation counts disadvantaged pupils placed by each school’s fitted pull on them, which reproduces the published shares for the cohorts admitted before the 2024 map and priorities, and assumes those pulls hold under today’s rules and when maps and schools change. Most options differ on the index by a few thousandths, which is inside what a change of measure has moved. And the academies and faith schools are modelled as responding to demand, not as making their own decisions about numbers. The Elm Grove runs were corrected in this version: competition is now measured from the Elm Grove site, and children refused elsewhere are re-offered places with the second preferences families gave shifted by how much the move changes each neighbourhood’s pull towards the school. Both raised Elm Grove’s figures a little. The site itself, and what building on it would cost, are not modelled. The direction of each finding is more reliable than its size.

text:
12.4 Licences, attribution and reuse
Most of this is Open Government Licence v3. The DfE, DfT, ONS, MHCLG and council datasets above are all published under OGL v3, which permits reuse with attribution. The attribution is in the table above.
OpenStreetMap is ODbL. The walking and road network under every routed journey time is © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database Licence.
The basemaps are Esri’s World Light Gray Canvas, used because it needs no API key. Every map carries the Esri and OpenStreetMap attribution in its corner, which the terms require, and R/99_verify_render.R fails the build if a map loses it. These tiles replaced CARTO’s, which are keyed: a render from a shell without the key produced watermarked maps and no other symptom, repeatedly.
The analysis is reproducible from these sources. R/01_assemble.R pulls every input into data/; R/02_accessibility.R and R/03_flow_regions.R build the accessibility surfaces and the redrawn catchments; the model outputs come from the open Brightopia bundle, which publishes its own code. What cannot be reproduced from this repository alone is the routed travel matrix, which needs an OSM extract and a GTFS feed and about an hour of compute — the matrix itself is carried in data/travel/, so nothing downstream of it requires the rebuild.






NoteWhat is deliberately not here



The council’s admissions records. Section 10.3 lists the releases that would replace a modelled flow with an observed one throughout sections 7 and 8. They are not public and this document does not use them.
Anything at individual level. The finest geography used anywhere is the postcode, and only for counts of households from the census. Every model input is at LSOA or catchment level.
Unpublished council material. Where a council figure is quoted it comes from a published report, a published factsheet or a determination of the Schools Adjudicator, and the section says which.

section: A system built for more children than it has
text:
A system built for more children than it has



The city publishes 2,515 Year 7 places across its ten secondary schools.
The modelled cohort is 2,267 in 2026 and 1,835 by 2035 — those children are already in primary school.
By 2035 that is about 720 empty Year 7 places a year.
Nine of the ten schools have been spending their reserves. The money is a city problem, not only a Longhill problem.


Longhill

Takes about 88 children in 2026 and 70 in 2030, on 210 places.
About £0.9m a year short of break-even in 2030.
Sits at the far edge of the city, at Ovingdean.

title: Brighton & Hove secondary schools
text:
What the evidence says

This is not mainly a school quality problem. Most of what separates schools’ headline results arrives with the children; the part a school can reach runs mostly through attendance.
Families choose on the headline score, which largely describes the intake — so choice is self-fulfilling.
Admissions criteria only bind at some schools. Several schools offer a place to every first-preference applicant.
Physical access is unequal, in the worst direction. 29 neighbourhoods can reach no school place within 30 minutes by walking and bus, and access and child poverty go together.
Concentrated disadvantage is not the harm it is assumed to be. Nationally, disadvantaged pupils do slightly better in schools with more of them, once absence and prior attainment are allowed for. Brighton Aldridge is the local example: its disadvantaged pupils leave with about 3 GCSE points more than comparable pupils elsewhere (four-year average; 5.7 in 2024-25).
Children from the most deprived neighbourhoods travel 3.4 minutes further each way than everyone else, under the map in force.

How to read an option


Compare in the same year. The cohort falls by a fifth by 2035. Read an option against doing nothing in that year.

title: Brighton & Hove secondary schools
text:
What to do

Lead with a smaller Longhill at the top of Elm Grove, with catchments redrawn round it — and test it properly, costs stated.
If the site cannot be had, return Whitehawk to Longhill’s catchment on its own.
Set Longhill at 150 on either site, and budget for the children it will get, not for 150.
Ask Cardinal Newman (300), King’s (150) and Brighton Aldridge (150) to take fewer, and every school to share the fall in proportion by 2030.
Trim Stringer, Varndean and Blatchington Mill only if Longhill stays at Ovingdean and only with a catchment redraw.
Publish where priority 6’s places went.
Ask the inequalities review to settle the measure — journeys or mixing — and whether journey length affects attendance, weighing the evidence that disadvantaged pupils do no worse where they are concentrated and well served.

title: Brighton & Hove secondary schools
text:
Next steps

Cost the Elm Grove site, and re-run the move on the council’s own records before deciding.
Draw the Elm Grove catchment with Rottingdean, Saltdean and Woodingdean in the room, before rather than after.
Check the disadvantaged-intake calibration against a second year of Year 7 offers.
Release ten small tables the council already holds — applicants’ home areas, full preferences, allocations, the criterion each place was given under, offers to children outside the city, and the catchment preference table for each year — which would turn most of the ranges here into estimates.
Link journeys to attendance in the council’s records, for the inequalities review.

A model calibrated to published catchment totals, not individual applications.
Catchment attachment carried to redrawn maps at the strength families follow the maps they have — the assumption every redraw result depends on.
Finances as a five-year steady state; site and capital costs not included.
The academies and faith schools modelled as responding to demand, not setting their own numbers.
The direction of each finding is more reliable than its size.

title: The model, stage by stage
section: 4.8 Corrected: Hove Park has two campuses
text:
4.8 Corrected: Hove Park has two campuses
Every school in the cost table sits where the school register puts it, which is the address the school gives. For Hove Park that address is the Nevill Campus on Nevill Road. But Hove Park teaches Years 7 and 8 at the Valley Campus on Hangleton Way, 1.65 km further west, and only moves pupils to Nevill Road in Year 9. This model is about Year 7. Every journey time it used for Hove Park was therefore a journey to a building the modelled children would not attend for two years.
The error is not random. The Valley Campus is west of the Nevill Campus, towards Hangleton and Portslade and away from central Hove and Brighton, so putting Year 7 at Nevill Road makes the school look nearer than it is to the parts of the city with most children in them, and further than it is from Hangleton. Routed to both sites, the Valley Campus is a median +9.2 minutes from the city’s neighbourhoods, but quicker from the 14% of them that lie west and north west.
This is temporary. The council gave statutory notice on 8 June 2026 to discontinue the Valley Campus on 31 August 2028 and consolidate the school on Nevill Road from 1 September 2028. So the model now carries both sites: entry years up to 2027 are taught at Hangleton Way, 2028 onwards at Nevill Road, and run_sim() picks the campus from the entry year unless told otherwise. Everything fitted to preferences or offers — attractiveness, the catchment terms, the competing-destinations term — is fitted with Year 7 at the Valley Campus, because every round it is fitted to was taught there.

tibble::tibble(
  Measure = c("Hove Park's intake",
              "Its mean journey",
              "Blatchington Mill's intake",
              "Portslade Aldridge's intake"),
  `Valley Campus` = c(
    sprintf("%.0f", hp_int(hp_v)),
    sprintf("%.1f min", hp_v$schools$mean_min[hp_v$schools$name == HPN]),
    sprintf("%.0f", hp_int(hp_v, "Blatchington Mill School")),
    sprintf("%.0f", hp_int(hp_v, "Portslade Aldridge Community Academy"))),
  `Nevill Road` = c(
    sprintf("%.0f", hp_int(hp_n)),
    sprintf("%.1f min", hp_n$schools$mean_min[hp_n$schools$name == HPN]),

About a quarter of the school’s intake changes ward. At Hangleton Way it draws heavily on Hangleton & Knoll, the ward it actually sits in, and on Portslade; at Nevill Road it draws instead on Westdene & Hove Park and Westbourne & Poets’ Corner. Those are different children, with different journeys and a different level of disadvantage, so every measure built on the composition of an intake — the segregation index, deprived children’s journey times, each school’s free-school-meal share — was being computed for the wrong families in the city’s largest paired catchment.






NoteWhat this does and does not fix



It does not fix Hove Park’s intake. The model still puts more children there than the school was offered in September 2026, and the reason lies elsewhere: most of Hove Park’s modelled intake is overflow refused at Blatchington Mill, and the city’s take-up of state places is not uniform (Section 2.9). Correcting the campus moves those children between wards rather than out of the school.
What it fixes is the geography, which everything downstream is built on. It also repaired a second fault it exposed: the out-of-city fit is a likelihood with more than one basin, and moving Hove Park was enough to send the optimiser into the wrong one, which cut the modelled flow from Longhill’s catchment to Priory School from about 35 children to almost none, at a likelihood six times worse. The starting grid is wider now and the fitted likelihood is reported, so the next time the geometry moves this shows up rather than passing silently.
Two things say the recovered basin is the right one rather than merely the better-fitting one. It reproduces the council’s published 2024 destinations — 38 children from Longhill’s catchment to Priory, against 35 modelled. And it puts them where local knowledge puts them: of the 45 children the model sends to Priory, 58% are from Woodingdean, the part of the city closest to Lewes, and the next largest share is from Rottingdean & West Saltdean. That outflow is a real feature of the eastern edge of the city and has no counterpart in the west, which is exactly why a badly-fitted version of it is easy to miss: nothing on the Hove side of the city would look wrong.

title: The Brighton Secondary School System
section: 5.5 Why Hove Park takes more disadvantaged children than Blatchington Mill
text:
5.5 Why Hove Park takes more disadvantaged children than Blatchington Mill
This question comes up repeatedly, and it is a good one. Hove Park and Blatchington Mill share a catchment and stand 0.5 km apart, yet Hove Park’s Year 7 is about 35.3% disadvantaged against Blatchington Mill’s 22.4% — a gap of 12.9 points between two schools with the same catchment and, on the face of it, the same geography.
The model can separate two explanations that are usually run together. The disadvantage layer has a term for each school, \(\lambda_j\), which is how strongly that school pulls the disadvantaged children of a neighbourhood it already draws from. Set every \(\lambda\) to one and each school simply takes its proportional share of each neighbourhood’s disadvantaged children: what is left is geography. The difference between that and the published shares is sorting within neighbourhoods.


Show code
hpc$gap %>%
  transmute(Treatment = case,
            `Hove Park` = paste0(hp_pts(hove_park), "%"),
            `Blatchington Mill` = paste0(hp_pts(blatchington), "%"),
            Gap = sprintf("%+.1f pts", 100 * gap)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrr")

Geography explains about 38% of the gap — roughly a third — and all of that comes from one thing: Year 7 is not taught at Hove Park’s registered address. It is taught at the Valley Campus on Hangleton Way, 1.5 km from Blatchington Mill and in Hangleton rather than central Hove. Put Year 7 at Nevill Road and the geographic part of the gap disappears entirely: -0.1 points, which is nothing. Two schools half a kilometre apart draw the same children, as you would expect.
The other two thirds is sorting, and the fitted \(\lambda\) is a measurement of it:

  arrange(desc(as.numeric(`Pull on disadvantaged children`))) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")

Hove Park’s 1.42 against Blatchington Mill’s 1.02 is the heart of it: from the same streets, Hove Park takes about 40% more of the disadvantaged children than its share of the intake implies. The two church schools sit at the other end — 0.51 and 0.62, so about half their proportional share — as do Varndean and Dorothy Stringer. Longhill is off the scale in the other direction.
That is the interaction worth naming. Closing King’s and Cardinal Newman in the model narrows the geography-only gap from 4.9 points to 3.5, so their pull is real but modest as a share of the whole. The larger effect is not that the church schools take children out of Hove Park’s catchment; it is that across the city the schools families compete hardest to enter take a smaller share of the disadvantaged children from every neighbourhood they serve, and the undersubscribed schools take the rest. Blatchington Mill fills; Hove Park takes those who did not get in, and those whose families did not name it first.

5.5.1 Will it even out when the Valley Campus closes?
This is the obvious follow-up, and it is a good theory: if the campus is what puts Hove Park’s Year 7 in Hangleton, bringing everyone to Nevill Road should bring the two schools together. The model’s answer is half right.


Show code
hpc$move %>%
  filter(year %in% c(2026, 2028, 2030)) %>%
  transmute(`Entry year` = year,
            `Hove Park` = sprintf("%.1f%% → %.1f%%", 100 * valley_dep, 100 * nevill_dep),
            `Blatchington Mill` = sprintf("%.1f%% → %.1f%%",
                                          100 * valley_dep_bm, 100 * nevill_dep_bm),
            `Gap` = sprintf("%.1f → %.1f pts", 100 * valley_gap, 100 * nevill_gap)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrr")

The gap narrows from 12.9 points to 6.7 — about 48% of it — and it closes from both ends, Hove Park falling and Blatchington Mill rising as the two swap children. But it does not disappear. Hove Park’s intake stays around 7 points more disadvantaged, because the part of the gap that is sorting rather than geography does not care where the building is. Moving a school changes which streets it draws from; it does not change which families name it first, or which school fills and which takes those who did not get in.
One caveat runs the other way, and it matters. \(\lambda\) is fitted over years when the school was split across two sites. If the split site is itself part of why families sort as they do — a lower school in Hangleton shaping what parents think they are choosing — then some of what the model counts as sorting would move with the building too, and more of the gap would close. The model holds that fixed by construction, so 48% is a floor, not a ceiling. Which of the two readings is right will be visible in the September 2028 and 2029 intakes.






WarningWhat this is, and what it is not



\(\lambda_j\) is fitted to reproduce each school’s published disadvantaged share. It measures sorting; it does not explain it. The model can say how much of the Hove Park–Blatchington gap geography accounts for — about a third, all of it the campus — and how much it cannot. It cannot say whether the remaining two thirds is parental choice, the order preferences are given in, the lottery, the priorities, or something else, and nothing here should be read as saying which.

title: The Brighton Secondary School System
section: 5.6 Does moving the school raise demand, or does the school have to change?
text:
5.6 Does moving the school raise demand, or does the school have to change?
The consolidation on Nevill Road in September 2028 is as close to a natural experiment as this system offers: one school, one known date, one move of 1.65 km east, with everything else held. The model’s answer:


Show code
hpc$move %>%
  transmute(`Entry year` = year,
            `At the Valley Campus` = sprintf("%.0f", valley),
            `At Nevill Road` = sprintf("%.0f", nevill),
            Difference = sprintf("%+.0f", nevill - valley),
            `Disadvantaged share` = sprintf("%.0f%% → %.0f%%",
                                            100 * valley_dep, 100 * nevill_dep)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrr")

The move is worth about +15 children a year, an intake 11% larger, and it holds as the cohort shrinks. It is not nothing: it is most of the difference between a viable form entry and an empty one.
But set it against the other lever. Staying at Hangleton Way and making the school 20% more attractive produces exactly the same intake. On this document’s own choice fit (Section 5.4), that multiplier is worth about 2.6 Attainment 8 points. Hove Park’s Attainment 8 is ; the highest in the city is 56.9. So the whole benefit of moving the school across Hove is about what a quarter of its gap to the top of the city would buy — and a single Attainment 8 point is worth roughly 7% more demand, or about 10 children.
The answer, then, is: the site helps, and the school’s standing matters more. The move is a one-off gain of a fixed size. Attractiveness has four times the headroom and compounds.
And there is a loop here that the model does not close, which is the most interesting thing in this section. The move itself makes Hove Park’s intake less disadvantaged — 36% to 31% in 2028 — purely because Nevill Road draws different streets. A less disadvantaged intake raises the school’s raw Attainment 8, because that is largely what raw Attainment 8 measures (Section 2.3). A higher headline score raises demand, because that is what families read (Section 5.4). Which raises the intake again.
That is the Longhill loop (Section 1) running forwards instead of backwards, and the consolidation may start it. Nothing in this model predicts it: \(W_j\) is fixed in every run above, so the figures here are the move without the loop. What they do establish is where to look, and the September 2028 and 2029 factsheets will show whether it happens. This is a prediction worth recording now, because a natural experiment is only useful if the prediction is written down before the result arrives.
